tool.name: Kubernetes
tool.tagline: Run and scale containerised applications across a cluster of machines
tool.description: Kubernetes is the open-source container orchestrator: you declare the desired state of your applications in YAML and its controllers keep the cluster matching it, scheduling containers, replacing failed ones, rolling out new versions and wiring up networking and storage. It is the common platform behind managed services such as EKS, GKE and AKS.

glossary.def: One computer (a real machine or a virtual machine) that is part of a Kubernetes cluster and runs containers for it.
The part of a Kubernetes cluster that makes the decisions: it stores what you asked for, picks where things run and keeps checking that reality matches.
What you have told Kubernetes should exist, such as 'three copies of this container'. Kubernetes keeps working to make what actually runs match it.
A program inside Kubernetes that watches one kind of object and keeps acting until what actually runs matches what you asked for, for example starting a replacement when a copy disappears.
What a controller does over and over: compare what you asked for with what actually exists, and make the changes needed to close the gap.
Reacting to how things are right now rather than to each individual change notification, so a missed notification does no harm: the next check sees the same state.
In Kubernetes, running several identical copies (replicas) of a pod, so the app keeps working if one fails and more users can be served.
In Kubernetes, one stored record describing something you want, such as a pod, a Deployment or a Service, with its name and settings.
The command-line tool for talking to a Kubernetes cluster: you use it to create, inspect, change and delete objects.
The control-plane program every other part of Kubernetes talks to. It checks each request, saves objects in etcd and tells watchers when they change.
The small, very reliable store, usually copied across several machines, that holds every object of a Kubernetes cluster. Only the API server talks to it.
The control-plane program that picks a node for every new pod, based on free CPU and memory and any placement rules.
The agent program on every node that starts the containers of the pods placed on that node, restarts them when needed and reports their state.
The program on a node that actually downloads images and starts and stops containers, such as containerd or CRI-O. The kubelet gives it its orders.
A program on each node that makes a Service's stable address work, by passing traffic sent to that address on to one of the Service's pods.
Container Network Interface: the kind of plugin that gives every pod its own network address and connects pods across nodes. Calico and Cilium are examples.
The smallest thing Kubernetes runs: one container (sometimes with a few helpers) sharing one network address and storage, always placed together on one node.
The settings file (usually ~/.kube/config) that tells kubectl which clusters exist, how to log in to them and which one to use now.
In Kubernetes, a named section of a cluster. Object names only have to be unique inside one namespace, and access rules and limits can be set per namespace.
The part of a Kubernetes object where you write what you want (its desired state). The cluster fills in a separate status part with what it actually sees.
A short name: value tag on a Kubernetes object, like app: web, used to find and group objects.
A rule that picks objects by their labels, such as app=web. Services and Deployments use one to find their pods.
A name: value note on a Kubernetes object for information that is never used to select it, such as who owns it or settings read by a tool.
The usual Kubernetes object for running an app: it keeps a chosen number of identical pods running and replaces them step by step when you change the version.
The object a Deployment creates for each version of its pods. It keeps exactly the requested number of matching pods running.
The part of a Deployment (or Job, StatefulSet...) that describes the pods it should create: their containers, images, settings and labels.
A Kubernetes object that gives a group of pods one stable name and address, and passes each incoming connection to one of the pods that is ready.
The default kind of Service, and its address: reachable only from inside the cluster, with each connection passed on to one of the Service's pods.
A kind of Service that also opens the same port on every node, so the app can be reached from outside the cluster through any node's address.
In Kubernetes, the address of one ready pod behind a Service; a Service's list of endpoints is kept in EndpointSlice objects. (For web APIs: one URL that does one job.)
A Kubernetes object listing the addresses of the ready pods behind a Service. Kubernetes updates it as pods come and go.
A Service with no address of its own (clusterIP: None). Looking up its name returns the addresses of its individual pods instead.
A container in a pod that runs to completion before the main containers start, for setup work such as waiting until a database answers.
A helper container that runs next to the main container in the same pod for its whole life, for jobs such as sending its logs elsewhere.
A pod status meaning its container keeps exiting: Kubernetes keeps restarting it, waiting a little longer after each crash.
The reason Kubernetes shows when a container was stopped by the Linux kernel for using more memory than it was allowed (exit code 137).
In Kubernetes, storage made available to a pod's containers as a folder. Some kinds last only as long as the pod; others keep data on a disk.
A Kubernetes object holding ordinary settings as name: value pairs, which pods can read as environment variables or as files.
A Kubernetes object holding sensitive values such as passwords and keys, given to pods as environment variables or files. By default the values are only encoded, not encrypted.
A temporary extra container you add to a running pod with kubectl debug, usually to bring debugging tools that the app's own image lacks.
A tool that runs a small one-node Kubernetes cluster on your own computer for learning and testing, with easy add-ons such as a web dashboard.
A Kubernetes object that caps the total CPU, memory and number of objects one namespace may use.
A Kubernetes object that sets default and maximum CPU and memory settings for each container in a namespace.
A Kubernetes object listing which connections to and from selected pods are allowed. Once a pod is selected, everything not listed is blocked.
Kubernetes replacing a Deployment's pods with a new version a few at a time, so some copies keep serving while the others are swapped.
A regular automatic check the kubelet runs against a container, such as asking it for a web page or running a command, to decide if it's ready or needs a restart.
A probe that decides whether a container may receive traffic now. While it fails, the pod is taken out of its Services; nothing is restarted.
A probe that decides whether a container is still working at all. If it keeps failing, the kubelet restarts the container.
A probe for slow-starting apps: until it succeeds, the readiness and liveness probes are switched off.
In Kubernetes, usually a resource request: the CPU or memory a container asks to have reserved on its node, used to decide where pods fit. (Elsewhere, a message asking a server to do something.)
Kubernetes' grouping of pods by how they set CPU and memory: Guaranteed, Burstable or BestEffort. It decides which pods go first when a node runs short of memory.
Kubernetes removing a pod from a node on purpose, for example because the node is short of memory or is being emptied for maintenance.
A cluster add-on that collects the current CPU and memory use of pods and nodes, used by kubectl top and by autoscalers.
A Kubernetes object with rules for web traffic from outside the cluster: which website name and path go to which Service. An ingress controller carries them out.
A program running in the cluster that reads Ingress objects and acts on them: it receives outside web traffic and passes it to the right Service.
The newer Kubernetes standard for outside traffic: Gateway objects describe the entry point, and route objects such as HTTPRoute say where requests go.
A Gateway API object with routing rules for web requests (website name, path, headers) and the Services they go to, optionally split by percentage.
Sending a new version to a small share of users first (say 10%) and widening it only if it behaves well.
A popular add-on that obtains TLS certificates for your sites, for example free ones from Let's Encrypt, and renews them before they expire.
The DNS server that runs inside a Kubernetes cluster and answers lookups for Service and pod names.
A suffix that name lookups add automatically to short names, so that inside a cluster api is tried as api.shop.svc.cluster.local.
A piece of real storage, such as a cloud disk, made available to the cluster. A PersistentVolumeClaim claims it for a pod.
A request for storage made for a pod: how much space and how it may be shared. Kubernetes finds or creates a matching PersistentVolume and binds the two.
A named kind of storage in a cluster, such as fast cloud SSD disks, telling Kubernetes how to create a new disk when a claim asks for one.
A setting of a storage claim saying who may use the storage at once: one node (ReadWriteOnce), one pod, or many nodes, read-only or read-write.
One of several separate data centres in a cloud region. Spreading copies of an app across zones keeps it running if one data centre fails.
A Kubernetes object like a Deployment for apps that keep data, such as databases: each copy has a fixed name (db-0, db-1...) and its own disk that follows it.
In Kubernetes, a program running in the cluster that runs one particular piece of software for you, such as a database, by reacting to objects that describe what you want.
A Kubernetes object that runs pods until a task finishes successfully, retrying failures, instead of keeping them running forever.
A Kubernetes object that creates a Job on a schedule, such as every night at 3am.
A Kubernetes object that runs one copy of a pod on every node (or every chosen node), used for per-machine helpers such as log collectors.
A mark on a node that keeps pods away unless they have a matching toleration, used to reserve nodes for special work.
A setting on a pod that allows it onto nodes with a matching taint. It permits, but doesn't attract.
Rules on a pod saying which nodes it must, or would prefer to, run on, based on the nodes' labels.
Rules placing a pod near (affinity) or away from (anti-affinity) other pods with certain labels, for example at most one copy per zone.
A rule asking the scheduler to spread an app's pods evenly across nodes or zones, so one failure can't take out most of them.
A Kubernetes object giving pods a priority number. When the cluster is full, higher-priority pods may push out lower-priority ones.
Evicting lower-priority pods to make room for a higher-priority pod that can't otherwise be placed.
A tool built into kubectl that makes per-environment versions of manifests by layering changes (overlays) on top of a shared base, without templates.
In Kustomize, a folder of changes for one environment (say prod) that is applied on top of the shared base manifests.
A small description of changes to apply to an existing file or object, such as 'set replicas to 6', instead of a full new copy.
A package manager for Kubernetes: it installs apps from charts, which are bundles of manifest templates with settings you can fill in.
Deploying from a git repository: a tool in the cluster keeps it matching what the repository says, so changes happen by committing to the repository.
A Kubernetes identity for programs running in pods, so their calls to the API can be given their own permissions.
A Kubernetes RBAC object listing allowed actions on kinds of objects inside one namespace.
Like a Role, but not tied to one namespace: used for cluster-wide objects or as a reusable set of permissions.
A Kubernetes object that gives a Role or ClusterRole to users, groups or ServiceAccounts within one namespace.
A Kubernetes object that gives a ClusterRole to users, groups or ServiceAccounts across the whole cluster.
A Kubernetes object that changes how many replicas an app has, adding pods when a measurement such as CPU use rises and removing them when it falls.
An add-on that watches how much CPU and memory pods really use, and suggests or sets better requests for them.
An add-on that scales apps on outside measurements such as the length of a work queue, and can scale them down to zero copies.
A tool that adds nodes when pods can't find room and removes nodes that sit mostly idle. Cluster Autoscaler and Karpenter are the common ones.
A set of network rules that blocks all traffic unless something explicitly allows it.
An extra layer of small proxies placed beside every pod that handles traffic between services: encryption, retries and detailed routing.
The part of a pod or container spec that sets its security options: which user it runs as, whether it can gain more rights, which files it can write.
Kubernetes' built-in check that rejects or warns about pods breaking a namespace's chosen security level: privileged, baseline or restricted.
The step where the Kubernetes API server checks, and may change or reject, a new or changed object before saving it, after checking who you are and what you may do.
Your own web service that the API server calls during admission, to change an object (mutating) or to accept or reject it (validating).
A Linux feature that filters which system calls (requests to the kernel) a program may make. The RuntimeDefault profile blocks rarely needed, risky ones.
Common Expression Language: short rules like self.minReplicas <= self.maxReplicas that Kubernetes evaluates to check objects.
A Kubernetes object saying how many of an app's pods must stay up (or may be down) during planned removals such as node drains.
To empty a node before maintenance: first cordon it (no new pods may be placed there), then evict its pods so they start on other nodes.
A pod removal someone chose, such as draining a node for an upgrade, as opposed to crashes and hardware failures.
A helper in Kubernetes' Go client library that lists and watches objects, keeps a local copy of them and tells the controller about every change.
A list of object keys (namespace/name) waiting to be reconciled. A key already waiting isn't added twice, and failed keys are retried later.
Writing without locking: each write says which version of the object it was based on, and is refused if someone changed the object in the meantime.
A link from a Kubernetes object to the object that created it, such as a pod to its ReplicaSet, so children are deleted with their owner.
In Kubernetes, the controller that deletes objects whose owner has been deleted, such as the pods of a deleted ReplicaSet.
A marker on a Kubernetes object that stops it being deleted until a controller has finished its clean-up and removed the marker.
Several copies of a program agreeing that only one of them, the leader, does the work at a time; if it dies, another copy takes over.
A small Kubernetes object used as a lock or heartbeat: a controller copy holds it to be the leader, and each kubelet renews one to show its node is alive.
An object that adds a new kind of object to the Kubernetes API, with a schema for checking it, so the cluster can store your own kinds of objects.
An object of a kind added by a CustomResourceDefinition, such as a Certificate or a Backup, rather than one built into Kubernetes.
A way of applying manifests where the API server does the merging and records which tool owns each field, reporting a conflict when two tools set the same field.
Container Runtime Interface: the standard way the kubelet gives orders to a container runtime, so Kubernetes works with containerd, CRI-O and others.
The shared environment set up for a pod before its containers start: its network and other Linux namespaces, held open by a tiny pause container.
Control group: a Linux kernel feature that groups processes and limits and measures their CPU, memory and other resources. Container limits are applied through it.
A virtual network laid on top of the real one: traffic between pods on different nodes is wrapped inside ordinary traffic between the nodes.
Network address translation: rewriting the destination (DNAT) or source (SNAT) address of network packets as they pass through a machine.
Linux's classic built-in system of rules for network packets, used by kube-proxy to send traffic for a Service's address on to a pod.
A Linux feature that runs small, checked programs inside the kernel, used by tools like Cilium to handle network traffic very quickly.
A popular way for programs to call each other's functions over the network. It keeps one long connection open and sends many requests through it.

concepts.name: What Kubernetes is for
concepts.summary: Kubernetes runs your containers across a group of computers and keeps them running the way you described.
concepts.why: Knowing the problem it solves tells you when it's worth learning and running, and when one machine with Docker is enough.
concepts.body:
Docker runs containers on one computer. A real service used by many people needs more: several copies of each container, spread over several computers, restarted when they crash, moved when a computer breaks, and updated to a new version without going offline. Doing all that by hand, at 3am, doesn't work. **Kubernetes** (often shortened to k8s) does it for you.

Kubernetes looks after a **cluster**: a group of computers that work together as one system. Each computer in it is called a **node**. You hand your containers to the cluster as a whole, and Kubernetes decides which node runs each one.

The central idea is that you describe the result, not the steps. Think of a thermostat: you don't switch the heating on and off yourself, you set 21° and it keeps the room there. In Kubernetes you write down "three copies of this image should be running". That description is the **desired state**, and this way of working is called **declarative**. The copies are called **replicas**.

Inside Kubernetes, programs called **controllers** keep comparing what is actually running with the desired state, and act to close the gap. If a node dies, the replicas on it vanish; a controller notices that only one of three is left and starts two more on other nodes. Nobody has to wake up.

You talk to a cluster with **kubectl** (often said "cube-control"), a command-line tool, much like you use the `docker` command. Usually you keep your descriptions in text files and hand them to kubectl, so the files themselves record how everything should look.

Kubernetes is worth it when you have:

- several services, several machines, or a need for updates without **downtime** (time when the app can't be reached) and automatic recovery,
- a team that wants one standard platform; cloud companies will run it for you (Amazon EKS, Google GKE, Azure AKS), or you can run your own.

For a single small app on one server, **Docker Compose** (Docker's tool for starting a few containers together on one machine) is far simpler.
concepts.code:
# The Docker way: you start one container; if it dies, that's your problem
docker run -d --name web nginx:1.27

# The Kubernetes way: ask for 3 copies; Kubernetes keeps 3 running
kubectl create deployment web --image=nginx:1.27 --replicas=3
kubectl get pods        # each copy runs inside a "pod" (see later lessons)
# NAME                   READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
# web-6d4cf56db6-2xk8p   1/1     Running   0          10s
# web-6d4cf56db6-7qv9z   1/1     Running   0          10s
# web-6d4cf56db6-mm5rt   1/1     Running   0          10s

kubectl delete pod web-6d4cf56db6-2xk8p   # remove one copy by hand
kubectl get pods        # a replacement appears within seconds
takeaways: You describe the desired state; controllers keep fixing reality to match it
A cluster is a group of computers (nodes); Kubernetes picks where each container runs
Worth it for several services and machines; overkill for one small app
pitfalls: Adopting Kubernetes for one small service where Docker Compose on a single server would do.

quiz.q: You asked Kubernetes for 3 copies of a container, then delete one copy by hand. What happens?
options: Kubernetes starts a new copy to get back to 3
Kubernetes deletes the other copies too
quiz.explain: The desired state still says 3, so a controller notices the gap and starts a replacement.

concepts.name: Cluster architecture
concepts.summary: The control plane decides what runs where; worker nodes run the containers. Every part talks through the API server.
concepts.why: When something breaks you need to know which part is responsible; this lesson is the map.
concepts.body:
A cluster has two kinds of nodes, a bit like a restaurant. The **control plane** is the manager's office: it keeps track of what was ordered and decides who does what. The **worker nodes** are the kitchen: they do the actual work of running your containers.

Kubernetes doesn't place loose containers on nodes. It wraps each container (sometimes with a small helper or two) in a **pod**, and the pod is what gets placed on a node. Pods have their own lesson; for now, think of a pod as "one running copy of your app".

Everything you ask for is saved as an **object**: a record describing one thing you want, such as "a pod running nginx:1.27". The control plane is a few programs that store these objects and act on them:

- The **API server** is the front desk. You, kubectl and every other part of Kubernetes send requests only to it. It checks each request and saves the objects. (An **API** is the set of requests a program accepts, and the agreed way to ask for them.)
- **etcd** is the cluster's filing cabinet: a small, very reliable store holding every object. Only the API server reads and writes it.
- The **scheduler** picks a node for each new pod that doesn't have one yet.
- The controller manager runs the built-in controllers you met in the last lesson, each watching one kind of object.

Each worker node runs:

- the **kubelet**, an agent that watches for pods assigned to its node and starts their containers,
- a **container runtime**, the program that actually starts containers (usually containerd, the same engine that runs underneath Docker),
- networking parts (**kube-proxy** and a network plugin, also called a **CNI** plugin) that give every pod its own address on the cluster's network and pass traffic to it.

The parts never call each other directly. They all read and update objects through the API server. The scheduler writes a node name onto a pod; the kubelet on that node notices and starts the containers.

When a cloud company runs Kubernetes for you, it runs the control plane; you see only your worker nodes.
concepts.code:
kubectl cluster-info
# Kubernetes control plane is running at https://127.0.0.1:6443

kubectl get nodes -o wide
# NAME            STATUS  ROLES          VERSION  INTERNAL-IP
# control-plane   Ready   control-plane  v1.35.0  172.18.0.2
# worker-1        Ready   <none>         v1.35.0  172.18.0.3

# On many clusters the control plane itself runs as pods,
# in a section called kube-system:
kubectl get pods -n kube-system
# etcd-control-plane, kube-apiserver-control-plane,
# kube-scheduler-..., kube-controller-manager-..., kube-proxy-..., coredns-...
takeaways: All parts talk only through the API server
etcd stores the objects; the scheduler picks nodes; controllers fix differences
The kubelet on each node turns assigned pods into running containers
pitfalls: Thinking the scheduler starts containers: it only writes the pod's node; the kubelet there runs it.

quiz.q: Which part actually starts a pod's containers on a node?
options: The kubelet, through the container runtime
quiz.explain: The scheduler only chooses the node; the kubelet on that node asks the container runtime to start the containers.

concepts.name: A local cluster with kind or minikube
concepts.summary: Run a throwaway Kubernetes cluster on your own computer to learn and test safely.
concepts.why: You learn Kubernetes by doing; a local cluster you can delete costs nothing and breaks nothing.
concepts.body:
You don't need a cloud account to practise. Two popular tools build a small cluster on your laptop:

- **kind** (short for Kubernetes in Docker) runs each node as a Docker container. It's quick to create, can easily have several nodes, and is popular on build servers that test code automatically.
- **minikube** runs a one-node cluster inside a virtual machine or a container, with easy optional extras such as a web dashboard.

Docker Desktop and Rancher Desktop can also switch on a built-in cluster from their settings.

You also need kubectl. Keep its version close to the cluster's: at most one version step apart, such as kubectl 1.34 with a 1.35 cluster.

With kind, creating a cluster is one command. A short settings file lets you ask for extra worker nodes.

Because kind's nodes are containers, each has its own image store, separate from your computer's. An image you just built with `docker build` isn't visible inside the cluster until you copy it in with `kind load docker-image myapp:dev`, or push it to a registry the nodes can reach.

When you're done, delete the cluster; a fresh one takes under a minute. If something gets into a strange state, recreating the cluster is usually faster than repairing it.

Local clusters differ from real ones in a few ways: there's only one control-plane node, storage is simple, and there's no cloud company to hand out public addresses. So one way of exposing apps, a Service of type LoadBalancer (covered later), stays waiting unless you add a tool for it.
concepts.code:
# kind-config.yaml: one control-plane node and two workers
kind: Cluster
apiVersion: kind.x-k8s.io/v1alpha4
nodes:
  - role: control-plane
  - role: worker
  - role: worker

# then, in a terminal:
#   kind create cluster --name dev --config kind-config.yaml
#   kubectl get nodes            # 3 nodes, Ready
#   kind load docker-image myapp:dev --name dev
#   kind delete cluster --name dev
takeaways: kind runs nodes as Docker containers; minikube offers handy extras
Copy local images into kind with kind load, or push them to a registry
Delete and recreate local clusters freely
pitfalls: Expecting an image you built locally to be available inside kind without kind load or a registry.

quiz.q: Your pod on a kind cluster shows ErrImagePull (Kubernetes couldn't download the image) for myapp:dev, which you just built with docker build. Most likely fix?
quiz.explain: kind's nodes have their own image store; copy the image into them (or push it to a registry they can reach).

concepts.name: kubectl and kubeconfig
concepts.summary: Use kubectl's get, describe, apply and delete commands, and switch between clusters with contexts.
concepts.why: kubectl is the tool you'll type all day; its patterns are worth learning once.
concepts.body:
kubectl needs to know which cluster to talk to and how to log in. It reads that from a settings file called **kubeconfig** (normally `~/.kube/config`). The file holds three lists: clusters (each with its API server's address), users (login details), and contexts. A context is a saved combination: this cluster, as this user.

- `kubectl config get-contexts` lists them; `kubectl config use-context prod` switches to the one named prod.

Clusters are often divided into named sections called **namespaces**, such as one per team or one per environment, so two teams can each have an app called `web`. A context can also remember which namespace to use when you don't say. Namespaces get their own lesson.

- `kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=shop` makes `shop` the default for the current context.

Commands follow one pattern: `kubectl <verb> <kind of object> [name] [options]`.

- `get pods` lists pods; `get deploy,svc` lists two kinds at once; `-o wide` adds columns; `-o yaml` prints the whole object; `-w` keeps watching for changes.
- `describe pod web-123` gives a readable summary plus recent events: short messages from Kubernetes about what happened to the object (placed on a node, image downloaded, failed to start). It's the first place to look when something is wrong.
- `apply -f file.yaml` creates or updates objects from a file (next lesson).
- `delete pod web-123` removes an object.
- `-n shop` picks a namespace, `-A` means all namespaces, `-l app=web` keeps only objects carrying that tag.

`kubectl explain deployment.spec.strategy` prints the documentation of any setting, straight from your cluster. `kubectl api-resources` lists every kind of object and its short name (`po`, `deploy`, `svc`).

Before running anything that deletes or changes things, check which context you're in. Many people show it permanently in their terminal.
concepts.code:
kubectl config get-contexts
# CURRENT  NAME      CLUSTER   NAMESPACE
# *        kind-dev  kind-dev  default
#          prod      prod-eks  shop

kubectl get deploy,svc -n kube-system
kubectl get pods -l app=web -o wide
kubectl get pod web-6d4cf56db6-7qv9z -o yaml | head -20
kubectl describe pod web-6d4cf56db6-7qv9z     # read the Events at the bottom
kubectl explain pod.spec.containers.ports
kubectl api-resources | grep -i deploy
# deployments  deploy  apps/v1  true  Deployment
takeaways: A context = a cluster + a user (+ a default namespace)
describe shows events; -o yaml shows the whole object
Check your current context before changing anything
pitfalls: Running kubectl delete or apply against production because the current context wasn't the one you thought.

quiz.q: Where do you look first to see why a pod is stuck in Pending (not started yet)?
options: The Events section of kubectl describe pod
quiz.explain: A pending pod has no running container that could print anything; the scheduler's reasons appear as events.

concepts.name: Manifests and kubectl apply
concepts.summary: Write the objects you want into YAML files (manifests) and let kubectl apply create or update them to match.
concepts.why: Files you keep and review like code are how real teams run Kubernetes; typed commands are forgotten by next month.
concepts.body:
Typing `kubectl create` commands is fine for experiments, but nobody remembers next month what was typed. Instead, teams write the objects they want into text files called **manifests** and keep them with the app's code.

Manifests are written in **YAML**, a plain text format of `name: value` lines. Indentation (spaces at the start of a line) shows what belongs inside what, and lines starting with `- ` are items of a list. Indent with spaces, never tabs.

Every object in a manifest has four top-level sections:

- `apiVersion`: which version of the Kubernetes API defines this kind of object, such as `v1` or `apps/v1`.
- `kind`: what it is: `Pod`, `Deployment`, `Service`...
- `metadata`: information about the object itself, such as its `name` and `namespace`.
- `spec`: the **spec** (short for specification) is the desired state. The cluster adds a `status` section with what it actually sees; you never write that part.

Several objects can share one file, separated by a line containing only `---`.

`kubectl apply -f web.yaml` creates the objects that don't exist yet and updates those that do, changing only what differs. It also works on a whole folder: `kubectl apply -f k8s/`. Because you state the result rather than the steps, this is the declarative way. Typing one-off commands such as `kubectl scale` is called **imperative**.

Useful habits:

- `kubectl diff -f k8s/` shows, line by line, what apply would change, before you do it.
- `kubectl apply --dry-run=server -f x.yaml` asks the API server to check the file without saving anything.
- Generate a starting file instead of typing one: `kubectl create deployment web --image=nginx --dry-run=client -o yaml > web.yaml`.

Each setting name, or **field**, is written in camelCase: words joined together, each new one capitalised (`containerPort`). A misspelled field is rejected by the API server with an "unknown field" error.
concepts.code:
# web.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: web
  labels: {app: web}
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels: {app: web}
  template:
    metadata:
      labels: {app: web}
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: nginx
          image: nginx:1.27
# shell:
#   kubectl diff -f web.yaml     # preview
#   kubectl apply -f web.yaml    # deployment.apps/web created
#   (edit replicas: 3)  kubectl apply -f web.yaml   # deployment.apps/web configured
takeaways: apiVersion, kind, metadata, spec; status is written by the cluster
apply creates or updates to match the file; diff previews the change
Generate a starting file with --dry-run=client -o yaml
pitfalls: Changing live objects by hand with kubectl edit, then losing the change on the next apply from your files.

quiz.q: Which section of an object should you never write in your manifest?
quiz.explain: status is what the cluster observes and reports; you write the spec.

concepts.name: Pods
concepts.summary: A pod is one or more containers that share a network address and storage and always run together on one node.
concepts.why: Every app on Kubernetes ends up as pods; knowing them explains addresses, restarts, logs and helper containers.
concepts.body:
A **pod** is the smallest thing Kubernetes runs. Most pods hold one container. When a pod holds several, they behave like programs on one small computer:

- They share one network address. Every machine on a network has an **IP address**, a number like 10.1.2.3 that others use to reach it, much like a phone number. Each pod gets its own.
- Inside the pod, containers reach each other on **localhost**, the name a computer uses for itself.
- They can share **volumes**: folders of storage attached to the pod.
- They always land on the same node, and start and stop together.

Extra containers are only for tightly linked helpers. An **init container** runs to completion before the app starts, for example waiting until the app's **database** (the program that stores its data) is answering. A **sidecar container** runs next to the app for its whole life, for example sending its logs elsewhere.

Pods are disposable. A pod is never moved: if its node dies, a controller creates a brand-new pod on another node, with a new IP address. That's why you almost never create pods yourself. You create a Deployment (or another controller object, met later), and it creates and replaces pods for you.

Main container settings: `image`, `command`/`args` (replace the start-up command that the image's Dockerfile set), `ports` (for documentation only), `env` (environment variables), `resources` and health checks.

A pod's phase is Pending (not started yet), Running, Succeeded, Failed or Unknown. The STATUS column of `kubectl get pods` adds detail such as `ContainerCreating` or **CrashLoopBackOff**: the container keeps exiting, and Kubernetes waits a little longer before each restart. `restartPolicy` (`Always`, `OnFailure`, `Never`) says whether the kubelet restarts containers that exit.
concepts.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: hello
  labels: {app: hello}
spec:
  initContainers:
    - name: wait-db          # waits until something named db answers on port 5432
      image: busybox:1.37
      command: ["sh", "-c", "until nc -z db 5432; do sleep 2; done"]
  containers:
    - name: app
      image: python:3.13-slim
      command: ["python", "-m", "http.server", "8000"]
      ports:
        - containerPort: 8000
# kubectl apply -f pod.yaml
# kubectl get pod hello      # Init:0/1 until db answers, then Running
takeaways: Containers in a pod share one IP address, localhost and volumes
Pods are disposable: a replacement is a new pod with a new address
Let controllers such as Deployments create pods for you
pitfalls: Putting two independent apps in one pod so they can talk on localhost: then they can't be scaled or updated separately.

quiz.q: Two containers in the same pod need to talk. What address works?
quiz.explain: Containers in a pod share one network address, so localhost reaches the other container's ports.

concepts.name: Labels, selectors and annotations
concepts.summary: Labels are name: value tags on objects; selectors use them to pick groups. Annotations hold extra notes.
concepts.why: Services and Deployments find their pods only through labels, so a wrong label quietly breaks things.
concepts.body:
A cluster soon holds hundreds of pods. To say "these ones", you tag them. **Labels** are short name: value tags in `metadata.labels`, such as `app: web`, `tier: frontend` or `env: prod`. By themselves they do nothing; they let people and other objects pick out groups.

A **selector** is a rule that matches labels:

- equality: `app=web`, `env!=prod`
- set-based: `env in (staging,prod)`, `tier notin (cache)`, `!beta` (has no beta label)

In kubectl: `kubectl get pods -l app=web,env=prod`. Inside objects, selectors are how things find their pods. A Deployment's selector picks the pods it owns. A **Service** (a stable address in front of a group of pods, two lessons from now) uses a selector to choose which pods receive its traffic.

The link is loose, and it's checked all the time, not just once. That's handy: change a pod's label and it immediately stops getting the Service's traffic, which lets you pull a misbehaving pod aside to investigate it. It's also a trap: two Deployments whose selectors match the same pods will fight over them.

Kubernetes recommends a set of common labels, such as `app.kubernetes.io/name` and `app.kubernetes.io/version`; installation tools fill them in for you.

**Annotations** look like labels but are never used for selecting. They hold notes: build information, the reason for a change, or settings read by other tools. They can be long; label values are limited to 63 characters.
concepts.code:
kubectl get pods --show-labels
# NAME        READY  STATUS   LABELS
# web-7f9-a   1/1    Running  app=web,pod-template-hash=7f9...
# api-5c4-b   1/1    Running  app=api,tier=backend

kubectl get pods -l 'app in (web,api)'
kubectl get pods -l tier!=backend

# take a pod out of its Service's traffic to investigate it
kubectl label pod web-7f9-a app=web-debug --overwrite
# its Deployment no longer counts it, so a replacement pod is created

kubectl annotate deploy web team=payments
takeaways: Selectors connect Services and Deployments to their pods
Equality and set-based selectors; -l on the command line
Annotations hold notes that are never used for selecting
pitfalls: Two Deployments whose selectors overlap, which then fight over each other's pods.

quiz.q: A Service sends traffic to pods with the label app=web. You change one pod's label to app=web-debug. What happens?
options: The pod stops receiving the Service's traffic
Nothing; selectors are checked only when the Service is created
quiz.explain: Selectors are checked continuously, so the pod drops out of the Service's list of targets.

concepts.name: Deployments and ReplicaSets
concepts.summary: A Deployment keeps N identical pods running through a ReplicaSet and manages the switch between versions.
concepts.why: It's the default way to run an app whose copies are all interchangeable, like most web services.
concepts.body:
A **Deployment** holds two things: a **pod template** (a description of the pods to create: containers, image, settings, labels) and a number of replicas. It doesn't manage pods directly. For each version of the template it creates a **ReplicaSet**, and the ReplicaSet's only job is to keep exactly that many matching pods alive.

So the chain is Deployment, then ReplicaSet (named like `web-5d8f7b9c4`), then pods (`web-5d8f7b9c4-4jx2l`). The middle part of the name is a short code computed from the template. Change the template (a new image, a new setting) and the code changes, so a new ReplicaSet is made. Change only the number of replicas, and the same ReplicaSet just grows or shrinks.

Rules of the spec:

- `spec.selector.matchLabels` must match the labels in `spec.template.metadata.labels`, and the selector can't be changed after the Deployment is created.
- `spec.template` is a pod spec, without its own `apiVersion` and `kind`.

Scale with `kubectl scale deploy web --replicas=5`, or by editing `replicas` in the file and applying it again. Prefer the file: otherwise the next apply from the file undoes your manual change. (Later you'll meet **autoscaling**, where Kubernetes changes the replica count by itself as traffic rises and falls; then leave the number out of your file.)

Deployments are for **stateless** apps: the copies keep no data of their own, so any replica can answer any user and can be replaced at any time. Apps that store data, like databases, use other objects you'll meet later (StatefulSets), as do tasks that run once and finish (Jobs).

`kubectl get deploy` shows READY (ready / wanted), UP-TO-DATE and AVAILABLE replicas.
concepts.code:
kubectl create deployment web --image=nginx:1.27 --replicas=3
kubectl get deploy,rs,pods -l app=web
# deployment.apps/web             3/3   3   3
# replicaset.apps/web-5d8f7b9c4   3     3   3
# pod/web-5d8f7b9c4-4jx2l   1/1   Running ...

kubectl scale deploy web --replicas=5          # same ReplicaSet, 2 more pods
kubectl set image deploy/web nginx=nginx:1.28  # new template: new ReplicaSet
kubectl get rs -l app=web
# web-5d8f7b9c4   0   0   0     (old version, kept so you can go back)
# web-7c6d9f8b5   5   5   5
takeaways: A Deployment manages ReplicaSets; ReplicaSets manage pods
Template change = new ReplicaSet; replica count change = same one
Use Deployments for stateless, interchangeable pods
pitfalls: Selector labels that don't match the template's labels: the API server rejects the Deployment.

quiz.q: Which change to a Deployment creates a new ReplicaSet?
options: Adding an annotation to the Deployment's metadata
quiz.explain: Only changes to the pod template produce a new template code, and so a new ReplicaSet.

concepts.name: Services
concepts.summary: A Service gives a group of pods one stable name and address, and spreads connections over the ones that are ready.
concepts.why: Pods come and go with new addresses all the time; Services are how anything reliably reaches your app.
concepts.body:
Pods are replaced all the time, and every new pod gets a new IP address. If one app had to keep track of another app's pod addresses, it would break constantly. A **Service** fixes this: it selects pods by label and gives the whole group one address that never changes.

Callers connect to the Service, and each connection is passed on to one of the matching pods that is ready. A Service also gets a name, such as `web`. The cluster's **DNS**, the system that turns names into IP addresses (like a phone book), lets other pods simply connect to `web`. Spreading connections over several copies like this is what a **load balancer** does.

Kubernetes keeps the current list of ready pods behind each Service in **EndpointSlice** objects, updated as pods come and go. Each pod address in that list is an **endpoint**.

Service types:

- `ClusterIP` (the default): an address reachable only inside the cluster. The workhorse for one app calling another.
- `NodePort`: additionally opens a port (30000-32767) on every node and passes it on to the Service.
- `LoadBalancer`: additionally asks the cloud company for an outside load balancer pointing at the nodes.
- `ExternalName`: just a second name for a host outside the cluster.

Ports: `port` is the one callers use on the Service; `targetPort` is the port the containers listen on.

A **headless Service** (`clusterIP: None`) has no address of its own: looking up its name returns the addresses of the individual pods. Apps that need to reach one specific copy use it.

For websites you usually don't give every Service its own LoadBalancer. One shared front door for web traffic (an Ingress or a Gateway, covered at the Practical level) sends visitors to the right ClusterIP Service.

`kubectl port-forward svc/web 8080:80` connects port 8080 on your laptop to the Service, which is perfect for testing.
concepts.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: web
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: web
  ports:
    - name: http
      port: 80          # callers use web:80
      targetPort: 8080  # the containers listen on 8080
# kubectl apply -f svc.yaml
# kubectl get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=web
# fetch the page from a temporary pod inside the cluster:
# kubectl run tmp --rm -it --image=busybox:1.37 -- wget -qO- http://web
# kubectl port-forward svc/web 8080:80   # then open http://localhost:8080
takeaways: A Service = a stable address and DNS name in front of the ready pods its selector matches
ClusterIP for inside the cluster; NodePort or LoadBalancer to reach it from outside
port is the Service's port, targetPort the container's
pitfalls: A selector that doesn't match the pods' labels: the Service exists but has no endpoints, so nothing answers.

quiz.q: A Service's name works, but every connection times out, and its EndpointSlice lists no addresses. Most likely cause?
options: Its selector matches no ready pods
quiz.explain: No endpoints means no ready pod matches the selector: wrong labels, or pods that aren't ready.

concepts.name: Namespaces
concepts.summary: Namespaces split one cluster into named sections, each with its own names, access rules and limits.
concepts.why: Teams and environments share clusters through namespaces, and many kubectl mistakes come from using the wrong one.
concepts.body:
A **namespace** is a named section of a cluster, like folders on a disk: two folders can each hold a file called `notes.txt`. You can have an app called `web` in namespace `shop` and another in `blog`. Most objects, pods included, live inside a namespace. A few belong to the whole cluster, such as nodes and namespaces themselves; `kubectl api-resources --namespaced=false` lists them.

Built-in namespaces:

- `default`: where things go if you don't say.
- `kube-system`: the parts of Kubernetes itself and its add-ons.
- `kube-public` and `kube-node-lease`: rarely touched.

Namespaces are the unit for several controls:

- Access rules: Kubernetes decides who may do what with **RBAC** (role-based access control). You define roles such as "can read pods" and give them to people. A role usually applies inside one namespace.
- Limits: a **ResourceQuota** caps the total CPU, memory and number of objects a namespace may use, and a **LimitRange** sets default limits for each container in it.
- Network rules: a **NetworkPolicy** says which pods may connect to which, and applies to pods in its own namespace.

Namespaces are not walls by themselves: pods in different namespaces can still connect to each other unless NetworkPolicies say otherwise, and they share the same nodes.

Deleting a namespace deletes everything in it. That makes temporary test environments easy to clean up, and makes `kubectl delete ns` dangerous.

Put `metadata.namespace` in your manifests or use `-n`; don't rely on the context's default for anything important.
concepts.code:
kubectl create namespace shop
kubectl get ns
kubectl -n shop create deployment web --image=nginx:1.27
kubectl get deploy -A              # all namespaces
kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=shop

# cap what the namespace may use in total
kubectl -n shop create quota team-quota \
  --hard=requests.cpu=4,requests.memory=8Gi,pods=40
kubectl -n shop describe quota team-quota
takeaways: Names must be unique within a namespace, not across the whole cluster
Access rules, quotas and network policies are set per namespace
Namespaces don't block traffic between pods by default
pitfalls: Assuming that pods in separate namespaces can't reach each other.

quiz.q: Which of these belongs to the whole cluster rather than to one namespace?
quiz.explain: Nodes (like namespaces themselves) are cluster-wide; pods always live in a namespace.

concepts.name: ConfigMaps and Secrets
concepts.summary: Keep settings and passwords outside the image and hand them to containers as environment variables or files.
concepts.why: The same image should run in every environment; only its settings should differ.
concepts.body:
An image should be the same in testing and in production; what differs is settings, such as which database to use or how much to log. Kubernetes keeps those outside the image, in two kinds of object:

- a **ConfigMap** holds ordinary settings as name: value pairs,
- a **Secret** holds sensitive values: passwords, access keys, and the keys a website uses to encrypt its traffic.

Both live in a namespace, and pods use them in two ways:

- as **environment variables**: one value with `valueFrom.configMapKeyRef` or `secretKeyRef`, or all of them at once with `envFrom`,
- as **files**: attach the object to the pod as a volume, and each name becomes a file whose content is the value.

Files are updated automatically, a short while after the object changes. Environment variables are read only when a container starts, so after a change you must restart the pods, for example with `kubectl rollout restart deploy/web`.

A warning about Secrets: by default their values are only **base64**-encoded. Base64 rewrites any data as ordinary letters and digits so it travels safely as text, and anyone can turn it back in one command. It is not **encryption**, which scrambles data so that only someone with the right key can read it. So protect Secrets in other ways:

- allow only the people and programs that need them to read Secrets,
- have the cluster's administrator encrypt the stored objects in etcd (cloud companies often do this already),
- never put real secret values in shared project files; keep them in a **secrets manager**, a secure vault service, and have a tool copy them into the cluster.

Create them from the command line: `kubectl create configmap app-config --from-file=app.conf` or `kubectl create secret generic db --from-literal=password=...`. In a manifest, `stringData` lets you write the plain value, and Kubernetes stores it encoded.

Mark a ConfigMap or Secret `immutable: true` if it should never change.
concepts.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata: {name: app-config}
data: {LOG_LEVEL: info, app.conf: "workers = 4"}
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata: {name: db}
stringData: {password: s3cr3t}      # stored base64-encoded
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata: {name: app}
spec:
  containers:
    - name: app
      image: busybox:1.37
      command: ["sh", "-c", "env; cat /etc/app/app.conf; sleep 3600"]
      env:
        - {name: LOG_LEVEL, valueFrom: {configMapKeyRef: {name: app-config, key: LOG_LEVEL}}}
        - {name: DB_PASSWORD, valueFrom: {secretKeyRef: {name: db, key: password}}}
      volumeMounts: [{name: conf, mountPath: /etc/app}]
  volumes:
    - {name: conf, configMap: {name: app-config}}
takeaways: Give containers settings as environment variables or as mounted files
Environment variables need a restart to change; mounted files update
Secrets are only encoded, not encrypted: limit who can read them
pitfalls: Saving Secret manifests with real passwords in shared project files because the encoded values look scrambled.

quiz.q: You update a ConfigMap that a pod reads through envFrom (as environment variables). When do its running containers see the new values?
quiz.explain: Environment variables are read when a container starts; restart the pods to pick up changes.

concepts.name: Logs, exec, events and port-forward
concepts.summary: Inspect running apps with kubectl logs, describe, events, exec, port-forward and temporary debug containers.
concepts.why: These commands answer most everyday 'why isn't it working?' questions.
concepts.body:
Your basic toolkit, roughly in the order you'll reach for it:

- `kubectl logs web-abc` prints what a pod's container wrote to standard output and standard error. `-f` keeps following, `--since=10m` shows only the last ten minutes, `-c name` picks one container in the pod.
- `kubectl logs web-abc --previous` shows the output of the previous run of the container: the one that crashed. When a pod is in CrashLoopBackOff, this is the log that explains why.
- `kubectl describe pod web-abc` shows the pod's state, how often it restarted, and why the last run ended, such as **OOMKilled**: stopped for using more memory than it was allowed.
- `kubectl events --for pod/web-abc` lists what the scheduler, the kubelet and controllers reported about it. Events are kept for only about an hour.
- `kubectl exec -it web-abc -- sh` opens a shell inside the container, if its image includes one.
- `kubectl port-forward pod/web-abc 8080:80` connects a port on your laptop to the pod, without making it reachable for anyone else.
- `kubectl cp web-abc:/tmp/dump.txt ./dump.txt` copies a file out (the container needs the `tar` program for this).

Some images are so stripped down that they have no shell and no tools at all. For those, `kubectl debug -it web-abc --image=busybox:1.37 --target=app` adds an **ephemeral container**: a temporary extra container, from an image full of tools, that joins the pod and can see the app's processes.

The node keeps logs only for the current and the previous run of each container. To keep history, teams send all logs to a central log system.
concepts.code:
kubectl get pods
# web-7f9c-x2   0/1   CrashLoopBackOff   5   4m

kubectl logs web-7f9c-x2 --previous      # output of the run that crashed
kubectl describe pod web-7f9c-x2 | sed -n '/Last State/,/Exit Code/p'
#   Last State: Terminated  Reason: Error  Exit Code: 1

kubectl events --for pod/web-7f9c-x2
kubectl exec -it deploy/web -- env | grep DB_   # check its environment variables
kubectl port-forward svc/web 8080:80
kubectl debug -it web-7f9c-x2 --image=busybox:1.37 --target=app -- sh
takeaways: logs --previous shows why the last run of a container died
describe and events explain placement and startup problems
kubectl debug adds tools to minimal images without rebuilding them
pitfalls: Reading the logs of the fresh container in a crash loop instead of the --previous one.

quiz.q: A pod restarts every minute. Which command most directly shows what the crashed container printed?
quiz.explain: --previous returns the logs of the previous (crashed) container instance.

concepts.name: Rolling updates and rollbacks
concepts.summary: Ship new versions without downtime using rolling updates, and undo bad ones with kubectl rollout undo.
concepts.why: Releasing safely and going back quickly is the main daily job Kubernetes does for you.
concepts.body:
When a Deployment's pod template changes, its controller performs a **rollout**: it scales the new ReplicaSet up and the old one down, a few pods at a time, so the app keeps serving throughout.

`spec.strategy` controls how:

- `RollingUpdate` (the default) with `maxSurge`, how many extra pods may exist above `replicas` during the change (default 25%), and `maxUnavailable`, how many may be missing (default 25%). `maxSurge: 1, maxUnavailable: 0` never drops below full capacity.
- `Recreate`: stop all old pods first, then start the new ones. Use it when two versions must never run at the same time.

Old pods are removed only as new ones become ready. Ready means the pod passes its **readiness probe**: a regular check, such as asking the app for its `/healthz` page, that Kubernetes runs to see whether it can take traffic (the Probes lesson covers it). Without one, a pod counts as ready the moment it starts, even if it's broken. `minReadySeconds` adds a waiting time after ready, and `progressDeadlineSeconds` marks the rollout as failed if it stalls; it does not go back automatically.

Commands:

- `kubectl rollout status deploy/web` waits for the rollout to finish and exits with an error if it fails, which suits automated releases (**CI/CD**: systems that test and ship every change without manual steps).
- `kubectl rollout history deploy/web` lists earlier versions (revisions, kept as old ReplicaSets, up to `revisionHistoryLimit`).
- `kubectl rollout undo deploy/web [--to-revision=3]` performs a **rollback** to the previous (or a chosen) version.
- `kubectl rollout restart deploy/web` replaces all pods with fresh ones with the same spec.
- `kubectl rollout pause` and `resume` let you make several changes and roll them out as one.

Remember that undo changes the object in the cluster, not your files. If your manifests still name the bad version, the next apply brings it back.
concepts.code:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata: {name: web}
spec:
  replicas: 4
  revisionHistoryLimit: 5
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate: {maxSurge: 1, maxUnavailable: 0}
  selector: {matchLabels: {app: web}}
  template:
    metadata: {labels: {app: web}}
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: web
          image: ghcr.io/acme/web:1.4.2
          readinessProbe: {httpGet: {path: /healthz, port: 8080}}   # ready = /healthz answers
# kubectl set image deploy/web web=ghcr.io/acme/web:1.5.0
# kubectl rollout status deploy/web --timeout=5m || kubectl rollout undo deploy/web
takeaways: maxSurge and maxUnavailable trade speed against spare capacity
Readiness decides when old pods go; rollout status fits automated releases
rollout undo changes the cluster, not your files
pitfalls: No readiness probe: pods count as ready the moment they start, so a broken version replaces all the good pods.

quiz.q: With replicas: 4, maxSurge: 1 and maxUnavailable: 0, how many pods can exist at most during a rollout?
quiz.explain: maxSurge 1 allows one pod above the desired 4, and none may go unavailable.

concepts.name: Liveness, readiness and startup probes
concepts.summary: Tell Kubernetes when a container is ready for traffic, when it is stuck, and how long it may take to start.
concepts.why: Probes are what make safe rollouts and automatic recovery real; badly chosen probes cause outages.
concepts.body:
The kubelet can run three kinds of **probe**, a regular automatic check, against each container:

- **readiness probe**: may this container receive traffic now? While it fails, the pod is taken out of its Services' endpoints; nothing is restarted. It keeps running for the container's whole life.
- **liveness probe**: is the container still working at all? If it fails `failureThreshold` times one after another, the kubelet **restarts** the container. Use it for an app that can get stuck forever (for example two parts each waiting for the other, a **deadlock**), not for one that's merely slow.
- **startup probe**: has the app finished starting? Until it succeeds, the other two are switched off. Use it for apps that start slowly, instead of a huge `initialDelaySeconds`.

Each probe is one of: an `httpGet` (ask for a web page; a status code from 200 to 399 is success), a `tcpSocket` (can a connection be opened?), an `exec` command (exit code 0 is success), or a `grpc` check for apps that use **gRPC** (a common way for programs to call each other over the network). Timing is set with `periodSeconds`, `timeoutSeconds` (default 1s), `failureThreshold` and `successThreshold`.

Good practice:

- Readiness checks what this pod needs before it can serve: for example, its start-up data is loaded and it accepts connections.
- Liveness should be cheap and check only the process itself. Never make it depend on a database or another service: if the database has a short hiccup, every pod's liveness fails at once and all of them restart together, turning a small problem into an outage.
- Give liveness a generous threshold; a restart is a heavy action.
- Many apps don't need a liveness probe at all, if they exit by themselves on fatal errors.
concepts.code:
containers:
  - name: api
    image: ghcr.io/acme/api:2.1.0
    ports: [{name: http, containerPort: 8080}]
    startupProbe:             # up to 30 x 5s = 150s to start
      httpGet: {path: /healthz, port: http}
      periodSeconds: 5
      failureThreshold: 30
    readinessProbe:           # may include dependency checks
      httpGet: {path: /ready, port: http}
      periodSeconds: 5
    livenessProbe:            # process-only check, generous
      httpGet: {path: /healthz, port: http}
      periodSeconds: 10
      timeoutSeconds: 2
      failureThreshold: 6
takeaways: Readiness: in or out of traffic; liveness: restart; startup: protects slow starts
Never make liveness depend on other services
Probe failures show up as events in kubectl describe
pitfalls: A liveness probe that checks the database, so a database outage restarts every pod over and over.

quiz.q: Your service takes 2 minutes to load its data at startup, and liveness restarts it before it finishes. Best fix?
options: Add a startupProbe with enough failureThreshold x periodSeconds
quiz.explain: A startup probe holds off liveness until the app has started, without making later failures slower to detect.

concepts.name: Requests, limits and QoS
concepts.summary: Requests reserve CPU and memory when placing pods; limits cap their use; together they set a pod's QoS class.
concepts.why: Wrong resource settings cause most mysterious OOMKills, slowdowns and pods that can't be placed.
concepts.body:
Each container can state `resources.requests` and `resources.limits` for `cpu`, measured in cores (`500m` means 500 thousandths, half a core), and `memory` (`256Mi`, `1Gi`).

- A **request** is what the container asks to have reserved. The scheduler places a pod on a node only if the node still has that much CPU and memory unreserved. When containers compete for CPU, it's also shared out in proportion to their requests.
- A limit is a hard ceiling, enforced by the Linux kernel. Going over the **memory limit** gets the container stopped: OOMKilled, exit code 137. Going over the **CPU limit** only slows the container down (it is "throttled"); it isn't killed.

How you combine them puts the pod in a **QoS class** (quality of service):

- `Guaranteed`: every container has requests equal to limits, for both CPU and memory.
- `Burstable`: some requests or limits are set.
- `BestEffort`: nothing set. These pods are the first to be removed, an **eviction**, when a node runs short of memory.

Practical advice:

- Always set a memory request, and a memory limit close to it: memory can't be taken back from a program the way CPU time can.
- Set CPU requests from measured use. Many teams leave out CPU limits, so busy services that must answer quickly aren't slowed down for no reason.
- `kubectl top pods` shows real use. It needs the **metrics-server** add-on, which collects these numbers.
- In a namespace, a LimitRange can fill in defaults and a ResourceQuota caps the total.

Some programming languages' runtimes (recent Java, Go, JavaScript on Node.js) read the container's limits and size themselves to fit. Check that yours does before relying on it.
concepts.code:
containers:
  - name: api
    image: ghcr.io/acme/api:2.1.0
    resources:
      requests:
        cpu: 250m        # scheduler reserves a quarter core
        memory: 512Mi
      limits:
        memory: 512Mi    # above this: OOMKilled
        # no cpu limit: may burst into idle CPU
# kubectl top pod -l app=api
# NAME        CPU(cores)  MEMORY(bytes)
# api-6f-x1   180m        430Mi
# kubectl get pod api-6f-x1 -o jsonpath='{.status.qosClass}'   # Burstable
takeaways: Requests decide placement; limits are enforced while running
Memory over the limit = OOMKilled; CPU over the limit = slowed down
QoS classes: Guaranteed, Burstable, BestEffort (evicted first)
pitfalls: Setting no requests at all: pods get packed onto nodes and are evicted or starved when load rises.

quiz.q: A container keeps exiting with reason OOMKilled. Which setting is it hitting?
options: Its memory limit (or node memory pressure)
quiz.explain: Going over the memory limit makes the kernel kill the process; using too much CPU only slows it down.

concepts.name: Ingress and the Gateway API
concepts.summary: Route outside web traffic to Services by website name and path, using an Ingress or the Gateway API.
concepts.why: One shared front door with encryption and routing rules is how websites are exposed, not a load balancer per Service.
concepts.body:
Web traffic uses **HTTP**, the language browsers and web servers speak; HTTPS is its encrypted form. The encryption is done by **TLS**, which needs a **certificate**: a digital ID card proving the site really is who it says.

An **Ingress** describes rules for web traffic coming from outside: website names (hosts), paths such as `/api`, and the Service each one goes to, plus TLS certificates stored in Secrets. An Ingress does nothing by itself.

An **ingress controller** is a program running in the cluster (Traefik, HAProxy, a cloud company's controller...) that watches Ingress objects and configures a **proxy** accordingly: a server that receives the requests and passes them on. `ingressClassName` picks which controller handles an Ingress. Many features (rewriting paths, time limits) live in controller-specific annotations, which is the Ingress design's weakness. The once-standard community ingress-nginx controller has been retired, so check what your platform supports.

The **Gateway API** is the newer, more capable standard and the recommended direction:

- `GatewayClass`: a kind of entry point, provided by an implementation (Envoy Gateway, Istio, Cilium, cloud controllers).
- `Gateway`: one actual entry point with its listeners (ports, protocols, TLS), usually owned by the platform team.
- **HTTPRoute** (and `GRPCRoute` and others): routing rules owned by app teams and attached to a Gateway. Matching on headers, splitting traffic by weight, redirects and rewrites are built in.

This split between the entry point and the routes, plus features that work the same everywhere, is why new setups tend to choose it. Its object types are installed separately from Kubernetes itself.

Splitting by weight enables a **canary release**: send, say, 10% of traffic to the new version, and raise the share only if it behaves.

For certificates, **cert-manager** can request free ones from Let's Encrypt and renew them automatically, for both Ingress and Gateway.
concepts.code:
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: HTTPRoute
metadata:
  name: shop
spec:
  parentRefs:
    - name: public-gw          # a Gateway run by the platform team
      namespace: infra
  hostnames: ["shop.example.com"]
  rules:
    - matches: [{path: {type: PathPrefix, value: /api}}]
      backendRefs:
        - {name: api, port: 80, weight: 90}
        - {name: api-canary, port: 80, weight: 10}   # 10% canary
    - backendRefs:
        - {name: web, port: 80}
# kubectl get httproute shop -o yaml   # status.parents shows Accepted / ResolvedRefs
takeaways: Ingress and Gateway need a controller to do anything
The Gateway API splits the entry point (platform team) from routes (app teams)
Weighted routes make canary releases possible without extra tools
pitfalls: Creating an Ingress in a cluster with no ingress controller, and wondering why nothing answers.

quiz.q: You applied an Ingress but nothing serves traffic, and its ADDRESS stays empty. Most likely cause?
options: The namespace is wrong for DNS
No ingress controller handles its ingressClassName
quiz.explain: An Ingress is only a set of rules; a controller must pick it up and report an address.

concepts.name: DNS and service discovery
concepts.summary: Pods find Services by DNS names like api.shop.svc.cluster.local, answered by CoreDNS inside the cluster.
concepts.why: Every call between services relies on cluster DNS; its search rules explain surprises across namespaces.
concepts.body:
Every cluster runs **CoreDNS**, a DNS server, in `kube-system`, and every pod's DNS settings file, `/etc/resolv.conf`, points at it. Each Service gets a full name:

`<service>.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local`

From a pod in namespace `shop`, all of these reach the `api` Service in `shop`: `api`, `api.shop`, `api.shop.svc`, `api.shop.svc.cluster.local`. From another namespace you need at least `api.shop`. Short names work because resolv.conf lists **search domains**: suffixes (`shop.svc.cluster.local svc.cluster.local cluster.local`) that are tried, in order, after a short name. Your own namespace comes first.

What a lookup returns (each answer is called a record):

- ClusterIP Service: an address record (A, or AAAA for IPv6) with the Service's address.
- Headless Service: one address record per ready pod and, for pods of a StatefulSet (a later lesson), fixed per-pod names such as `db-0.db.shop.svc.cluster.local`.
- Named ports also get SRV records, which carry port numbers.

A cost to know: resolv.conf also says `ndots:5`. Any name with fewer than five dots, such as `api.github.com`, is first tried with each search suffix, so one lookup becomes several wasted ones. For outside names you call very often, add a final dot (`api.github.com.`), which means "this name is complete", or lower `ndots` in the pod's `dnsConfig`.

Kubernetes also puts `<SERVICE>_SERVICE_HOST` and `_PORT` environment variables into pods, for Services that already existed when the pod started. DNS is preferred because it doesn't depend on what was created first.
concepts.code:
kubectl -n shop run dns --rm -it --image=busybox:1.37 -- sh
/ # cat /etc/resolv.conf
# search shop.svc.cluster.local svc.cluster.local cluster.local
# nameserver 10.96.0.10
# options ndots:5
/ # nslookup api                      # same namespace
# Name:   api.shop.svc.cluster.local
# Address: 10.96.112.7
/ # nslookup postgres.data            # Service postgres in namespace data
/ # nslookup db-0.db.data.svc.cluster.local   # one StatefulSet pod
takeaways: Service names: name.namespace.svc.cluster.local
Short names work only within the same namespace
Headless Services return pod addresses; ndots:5 adds lookups for outside names
pitfalls: Calling http://api from another namespace and getting NXDOMAIN (no such name); use api.<namespace>.

quiz.q: A pod in namespace web calls http://db:5432, but the db Service lives in namespace data. What happens?
options: Name resolution fails unless web also has a db Service
DNS returns all db pods in all namespaces
quiz.explain: Short names are tried with the pod's own namespace first, so db becomes db.web.svc..., which doesn't exist.

concepts.name: Volumes, PersistentVolumes and claims
concepts.summary: Pods ask for lasting storage with a PersistentVolumeClaim; a StorageClass creates the actual disk.
concepts.why: A container's own files are lost when it's replaced; anything that must survive needs a volume.
concepts.body:
A pod's `volumes` list makes storage available, and each container chooses where to see it with `volumeMounts`. Some volume types are temporary: `emptyDir` lasts as long as the pod (scratch space, or files shared between its containers), and `configMap` or `secret` volumes present settings as files.

For data that must survive, Kubernetes separates asking for storage from supplying it:

- A **PersistentVolumeClaim** (PVC, lives in a namespace) asks for storage: a size, an access mode and, optionally, a storage class.
- A **PersistentVolume** (PV, cluster-wide) is a real piece of storage: a cloud disk, or a shared folder on the network (NFS).
- A **StorageClass** names a kind of storage and the **driver** that creates it: a storage plugin (a CSI driver) for a cloud's disks (AWS EBS, Google Persistent Disk, Azure Disk) or for software such as Longhorn. With dynamic **provisioning**, creating a PVC makes the driver create a disk and a PV automatically, and binds the two together.

**Access modes** say who may use the storage at once: `ReadWriteOnce` (one node at a time; typical cloud disks), `ReadWriteOncePod` (one pod), `ReadOnlyMany`, `ReadWriteMany` (shared network folders such as NFS or AWS EFS).

`reclaimPolicy` says what happens when the PVC is deleted: `Delete` (the default for automatically created disks: the disk and its data are gone) or `Retain`.

Clouds split each region into **availability zones**, separate data centres, and a cloud disk can be attached only within its own zone. `volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer` therefore waits to create the disk until a pod using it has been placed, so the disk is made in that pod's zone.

You can usually grow a PVC by raising its size, if the StorageClass has `allowVolumeExpansion: true`. You can't shrink one.
concepts.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata: {name: uploads}
spec:
  accessModes: [ReadWriteOnce]
  storageClassName: standard     # kubectl get storageclass
  resources:
    requests: {storage: 10Gi}
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata: {name: uploader}
spec:
  containers:
    - name: app
      image: busybox:1.37
      command: ["sh", "-c", "date >> /data/log; sleep 3600"]
      volumeMounts: [{name: data, mountPath: /data}]
  volumes:
    - name: data
      persistentVolumeClaim: {claimName: uploads}
# kubectl get pvc uploads     # STATUS Bound, VOLUME pvc-3f1c...
takeaways: PVC = request, PV = the actual storage, StorageClass = how to create it
ReadWriteOnce disks attach to one node at a time
The default reclaimPolicy Delete removes the disk with the PVC
pitfalls: Scaling a Deployment with one ReadWriteOnce PVC to several replicas on different nodes: the extra pods can't mount it.

quiz.q: Why is WaitForFirstConsumer useful for cloud disks that can only be used in one availability zone?
options: It creates the disk only once the pod's node, and so its zone, is known
quiz.explain: Creating the disk before the pod is placed might put it in a zone where the pod can't run.

concepts.name: StatefulSets
concepts.summary: Run apps that keep data with stable pod names, stable DNS names and their own volume per replica.
concepts.why: Databases and other software that keeps data need an identity and storage that survive being moved.
concepts.body:
A **StatefulSet** is like a Deployment, but each replica has a lasting identity:

- **Stable names**: `db-0`, `db-1`, `db-2`. The number is the replica's ordinal, its position in the set. A replacement for `db-1` is again `db-1`.
- **Stable DNS names** through a headless Service named in `serviceName`: `db-0.db.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local`.
- **Stable storage** through `volumeClaimTemplates`: each replica gets its own PVC (`data-db-0`, `data-db-1`) that follows it to whichever node it's placed on next.
- **Order**: by default pods are created one at a time (0, then 1, then 2) and removed in reverse. `podManagementPolicy: Parallel` relaxes this.

Updates go from the highest ordinal down. `updateStrategy.rollingUpdate.partition: N` updates only pods numbered N or above, an easy way to try a new version on one replica first.

Scaling down does **not** delete the PVCs by default, so data survives a mistaken scale-down; `persistentVolumeClaimRetentionPolicy` changes that.

A StatefulSet gives identity, not teamwork. The software itself still has to copy data between replicas, agree which one is the leader that accepts writes, and switch to another if the leader dies (**failover**).

Running production databases on Kubernetes is very doable, usually through an **operator**: a program in the cluster that knows how to run one particular database (CloudNativePG for PostgreSQL, Strimzi for the Kafka messaging system) and carries out its procedures for you. Or simply use a database run for you by your cloud company.
concepts.code:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: StatefulSet
metadata: {name: db}
spec:
  serviceName: db            # headless Service (clusterIP: None) named db
  replicas: 3
  selector: {matchLabels: {app: db}}
  template:
    metadata: {labels: {app: db}}
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: postgres
          image: postgres:17
          env: [{name: POSTGRES_PASSWORD, valueFrom: {secretKeyRef: {name: db, key: password}}}]
          volumeMounts: [{name: data, mountPath: /var/lib/postgresql/data}]
  volumeClaimTemplates:
    - metadata: {name: data}
      spec:
        accessModes: [ReadWriteOnce]
        resources: {requests: {storage: 20Gi}}
# pods: db-0, db-1, db-2   PVCs: data-db-0, data-db-1, data-db-2
takeaways: Stable numbered names, DNS names and a PVC per replica
Needs a headless Service named in serviceName
PVCs survive scale-down; copying data between replicas is still the software's job
pitfalls: Expecting three StatefulSet replicas of Postgres to copy data between themselves automatically.

quiz.q: Pod db-1 of a StatefulSet is deleted. What does its replacement get?
options: A random name and a new empty volume
The name db-1 and the same PVC data-db-1
It isn't replaced until you scale
quiz.explain: StatefulSet replicas keep their numbered identity and get their own claim (PVC) back.

concepts.name: Jobs and CronJobs
concepts.summary: Run tasks to completion with Jobs, with retries and parallel pods, and on a schedule with CronJobs.
concepts.why: Database updates, bulk processing and nightly reports need tasks that run to completion, not always-on pods.
concepts.body:
A **Job** creates pods until a given number of them finish successfully. Its pods use `restartPolicy: OnFailure` or `Never`, since they're meant to end.

- `completions`: how many successful pods are needed (default 1).
- `parallelism`: how many run at once.
- `completionMode: Indexed`: each pod gets its own number in `JOB_COMPLETION_INDEX`, handy for splitting work into slices.
- `backoffLimit`: how many retries before the Job is marked failed (default 6). Retries wait longer each time (**exponential backoff**).
- `activeDeadlineSeconds`: a hard time limit.
- `ttlSecondsAfterFinished`: delete the Job and its pods automatically this long after it ends.

A **CronJob** creates a Job on a schedule written in cron syntax, the classic Unix format for repeating times: `"0 3 * * *"` means minute 0 of hour 3, every day. `timeZone` (e.g. `"Europe/Berlin"`) says whose 3am. Important settings:

- `concurrencyPolicy`: `Allow`, `Forbid` (skip a run if the previous one is still going) or `Replace`.
- `startingDeadlineSeconds`: how late a missed run may still start.
- `successfulJobsHistoryLimit` / `failedJobsHistoryLimit`: how many finished Jobs to keep.

Jobs can do the same work more than once: a pod may be retried after finishing part of its work, and a CronJob can occasionally create two Jobs for one time slot. So make the work **idempotent**: running it twice must have the same effect as running it once.

Start a CronJob's task by hand with `kubectl create job --from=cronjob/report report-manual`.
concepts.code:
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: CronJob
metadata: {name: nightly-report}
spec:
  schedule: "0 3 * * *"
  timeZone: "Europe/Berlin"
  concurrencyPolicy: Forbid
  jobTemplate:
    spec:
      backoffLimit: 3
      activeDeadlineSeconds: 1800
      ttlSecondsAfterFinished: 86400
      template:
        spec:
          restartPolicy: OnFailure
          containers:
            - name: report
              image: ghcr.io/acme/report:1.2.0
              args: ["--date", "yesterday"]
# kubectl create job --from=cronjob/nightly-report test-run
# kubectl get jobs -w      # COMPLETIONS 1/1
takeaways: Jobs retry up to backoffLimit and finish once enough pods succeed
CronJobs: schedule, timeZone, concurrencyPolicy
Make job work idempotent: it can run more than once
pitfalls: Leaving restartPolicy at Always in a Job's pod template: the API server rejects it.
