quiz.q: A nightly CronJob sometimes runs longer than 24 hours and two runs overlap. Which setting prevents that?
quiz.explain: Forbid skips a new run while the previous Job is still active.

concepts.name: DaemonSets
concepts.summary: Run one copy of a pod on every node (or chosen nodes) for helpers like log collectors and network plugins.
concepts.why: Per-machine helpers for logs, measurements, networking and storage are all DaemonSets.
concepts.body:
A **DaemonSet** makes sure one copy of a pod runs on each eligible node. When a node joins the cluster it gets one; when the node leaves, the pod goes with it. There's no `replicas` field.

Typical uses are helpers that every machine needs:

- log collectors (such as Fluent Bit) reading the node's `/var/log` folder,
- agents that measure each node's CPU, memory and disk use (node-exporter, the Datadog agent),
- network plugins (Cilium, Calico) and kube-proxy,
- storage plugins that attach disks on each node.

To run it only on some nodes, put a `nodeSelector` (node labels that must match) or node affinity rules in the pod template: for example only nodes with graphics processors (**GPUs**), or only Linux nodes.

Some nodes carry a **taint**, a mark that keeps pods away: control-plane nodes, for example, or nodes reserved for special work. A pod may go there only if it has a matching **toleration**. Agents that must run everywhere usually tolerate every taint.

DaemonSet pods often need access to the node itself: `hostPath` volumes (a folder of the node), `hostNetwork: true` (the node's own network), or extra privileges. Grant only what's needed; attackers love these pods.

Updates use `RollingUpdate` with `maxUnavailable` (default: one node at a time), or `OnDelete`, which updates a node's pod only when you delete it by hand.

Set resource requests carefully: they're reserved on every node, so 200Mi on 100 nodes adds up.
concepts.code:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: DaemonSet
metadata: {name: node-logs, namespace: logging}
spec:
  selector: {matchLabels: {app: node-logs}}
  template:
    metadata: {labels: {app: node-logs}}
    spec:
      tolerations:
        - {operator: Exists}            # run on tainted nodes too
      containers:
        - name: fluent-bit
          image: fluent/fluent-bit:4.0
          resources: {requests: {cpu: 50m, memory: 64Mi}, limits: {memory: 128Mi}}
          volumeMounts: [{name: varlog, mountPath: /var/log, readOnly: true}]
      volumes:
        - {name: varlog, hostPath: {path: /var/log}}
# kubectl -n logging get ds node-logs   # DESIRED = number of nodes
takeaways: One pod per eligible node; follows nodes in and out
Use nodeSelector or affinity to choose nodes, tolerations to reach tainted ones
Requests are paid on every node
pitfalls: Forgetting tolerations, so the agent silently skips tainted nodes.

quiz.q: A new node joins the cluster. What does a DaemonSet do?
options: Schedules its pod onto the new node if eligible
Moves an existing pod to it
quiz.explain: DaemonSets track nodes and add a pod to each new eligible node.

concepts.name: Kustomize overlays
concepts.summary: Make per-environment versions of plain YAML with a base, overlays and patches, built into kubectl.
concepts.why: You need dev, staging and prod variants of the same manifests without copy-pasting them.
concepts.body:
**Kustomize** builds final manifests from a `kustomization.yaml` file. Unlike tools that use a **template** (a file with blanks to fill in), it keeps your files as normal, valid Kubernetes YAML and layers changes on top. It's built into kubectl: `kubectl apply -k dir/` applies the result, and `kubectl kustomize dir/` prints it.

The usual layout is a base folder with the shared manifests, and an **overlay** folder per environment (dev, staging, prod) that refers to the base and adds its own changes:

- `resources`: files or folders to include (an overlay lists the base).
- `namespace`, `namePrefix`/`nameSuffix`, `labels`: applied to every object.
- `images`: change image names or tags without touching the Deployment.
- `replicas`: change replica counts.
- `patches`: a **patch** is a small description of a change ("add these resource settings to the first container"); Kustomize accepts two formats, for anything the shortcuts above don't cover.
- `configMapGenerator` / `secretGenerator`: build ConfigMaps or Secrets from files or values. They add a short code computed from the content to the name and update every reference to it, so changing the settings changes the pod template and automatically rolls out new pods.

Kustomize or **Helm**? Helm is a package manager for Kubernetes: it installs apps from charts, bundles of templated manifests with settings others can fill in. Kustomize suits your own apps' differences between environments, and patching YAML you got from someone else; Helm suits handing configurable apps to others. Many teams use both, for example patching a Helm chart's output with Kustomize.

Automated deploy systems understand Kustomize folders directly, including **GitOps** tools (Argo CD, Flux), which keep a cluster matching what a git repository says.
concepts.code:
# base/kustomization.yaml
resources: [deployment.yaml, service.yaml]

# overlays/prod/kustomization.yaml
resources: [../../base]
namespace: shop-prod
images:
  - name: ghcr.io/acme/web
    newTag: "1.5.0"
replicas:
  - {name: web, count: 6}
configMapGenerator:
  - name: web-config
    literals: [LOG_LEVEL=warn]
patches:
  - target: {kind: Deployment, name: web}
    patch: |-
      - op: add
        path: /spec/template/spec/containers/0/resources
        value: {requests: {cpu: 500m, memory: 1Gi}}
# kubectl kustomize overlays/prod | less ; kubectl apply -k overlays/prod
takeaways: A base plus one overlay per environment, no templates
images, replicas, patches and configMapGenerator cover most changes
Generated ConfigMaps get a content code in their name, so changes roll out new pods
pitfalls: Copying the whole base into each environment instead of patching only the differences.

quiz.q: Why does configMapGenerator add a short code computed from the content (a hash) to the ConfigMap's name?
options: To avoid name collisions between namespaces
So that content changes alter the pod template and roll out new pods
Because ConfigMap names must be unique cluster-wide
quiz.explain: The new name is written into the Deployment, which changes its pod template and rolls out new pods.

concepts.name: RBAC and service accounts
concepts.summary: Give people and programs exactly the API permissions they need with Roles, ClusterRoles and bindings.
concepts.why: Without tight RBAC, any hijacked pod or stolen laptop login can do anything in the cluster.
concepts.body:
Every request to the API server is made by a subject: a user (whose identity comes from your company's login system or from a **certificate**, a digital ID card), a group, or a **ServiceAccount**, an identity for programs running in pods. RBAC decides what the subject may do. Permissions only add up; there are no "deny" rules.

- A **Role** lists rules within one namespace: API groups, kinds of object (`resources`) and actions (`verbs`: `get`, `list`, `watch`, `create`, `update`, `patch`, `delete`), optionally only for named objects.
- A **ClusterRole** is the same, but not tied to a namespace: for cluster-wide objects, or as a reusable set of rules.
- A **RoleBinding** gives a Role or ClusterRole to subjects within one namespace.
- A **ClusterRoleBinding** gives a ClusterRole across the whole cluster.

The built-in ClusterRoles `view`, `edit` and `admin` cover common needs; give them per namespace with a RoleBinding.

Pods run as their namespace's `default` ServiceAccount unless you set `serviceAccountName`. The account's **token**, a string the pod sends to prove who it is, is placed in the pod as a file; it's short-lived and replaced automatically. Set `automountServiceAccountToken: false` when a pod never calls the API.

Check permissions with `kubectl auth can-i list secrets -n shop --as=system:serviceaccount:shop:web`.

Dangerous grants: `list` or `get` on Secrets; `create` on pods (a new pod can read any Secret in its namespace or run with full privileges); `escalate` and `bind`; `impersonate` (act as someone else); and `*` wildcards, which mean "everything".
concepts.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata: {name: deployer, namespace: shop}
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: Role
metadata: {name: deploy-updater, namespace: shop}
rules:
  - apiGroups: ["apps"]
    resources: ["deployments"]
    verbs: ["get", "list", "patch"]
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata: {name: deployer-can-update, namespace: shop}
subjects:
  - {kind: ServiceAccount, name: deployer, namespace: shop}
roleRef: {kind: Role, name: deploy-updater, apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io}
# kubectl auth can-i patch deploy -n shop --as=system:serviceaccount:shop:deployer  # yes
# kubectl auth can-i delete deploy -n shop --as=system:serviceaccount:shop:deployer # no
takeaways: Roles and ClusterRoles say what; bindings say who and where
RBAC only adds permissions: there are no deny rules
kubectl auth can-i --as tests what any subject may do
pitfalls: Giving an automated deploy pipeline's ServiceAccount cluster-admin (full control) because a narrower Role took effort.

quiz.q: You want a ClusterRole's rules to apply in only one namespace. What do you create?
options: A copy as a namespaced Role is the only way
A RoleBinding in that namespace referencing the ClusterRole
quiz.explain: A RoleBinding can reference a ClusterRole and grants it only within its own namespace.

concepts.name: Autoscaling: HPA, VPA and nodes
concepts.summary: Scale pod counts on measurements with the HorizontalPodAutoscaler, right-size requests with VPA, and add nodes automatically.
concepts.why: Traffic rises and falls; autoscaling keeps response times steady without paying for peak capacity all day.
concepts.body:
Three layers of autoscaling work together:

- The **HorizontalPodAutoscaler** (HPA) changes a Deployment's or StatefulSet's `replicas` to keep a measurement near a target. CPU and memory use are measured **as a percentage of requests**, from metrics-server.
- Other measurements, such as the number of waiting messages in a queue or requests per second, come through an adapter such as Prometheus Adapter (Prometheus is a popular monitoring system) or **KEDA**, which can also scale an app down to zero pods.
- The **VerticalPodAutoscaler** (VPA, an add-on) suggests or applies better requests based on what pods really use. Don't let VPA and HPA both react to CPU for the same app; they'll fight.
- A **node autoscaler** (Cluster Autoscaler or Karpenter) adds nodes when pods stay Pending for lack of room, and removes nodes that are mostly idle.

HPA details that matter:

- It needs resource requests; without them it can't compute a percentage.
- `minReplicas` and `maxReplicas` set the bounds.
- `behavior` controls how fast it scales. Scaling down waits five minutes by default (a "stabilisation window") so the count doesn't flap up and down.
- Remove `replicas` from your Deployment manifest, or every apply will reset what the HPA chose.

The rule is roughly `desired = ceil(current * currentMetric / target)`, where ceil rounds up. Scaling only reacts after load has risen, and new pods take time to start, so keep some spare capacity and make startup fast.
concepts.code:
apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
metadata: {name: api}
spec:
  scaleTargetRef: {apiVersion: apps/v1, kind: Deployment, name: api}
  minReplicas: 3
  maxReplicas: 30
  metrics:
    - type: Resource
      resource:
        name: cpu
        target: {type: Utilization, averageUtilization: 70}  # % of requests
  behavior:
    scaleDown:
      stabilizationWindowSeconds: 300
      policies: [{type: Percent, value: 50, periodSeconds: 60}]
# kubectl get hpa api
# NAME  REFERENCE       TARGETS       MINPODS  MAXPODS  REPLICAS
# api   Deployment/api  cpu: 85%/70%  3        30       4
takeaways: The HPA scales replicas on measurements relative to requests
KEDA and adapters scale on queues or traffic
Node autoscalers add nodes when pods are Pending
pitfalls: Keeping replicas: 3 in the Deployment manifest so every deploy resets what the HPA chose.

quiz.q: 4 pods average 90% CPU utilisation against a 60% target. Roughly how many replicas will the HPA want?

concepts.name: Scheduling: affinity, taints and spread
concepts.summary: Steer pods onto or away from nodes with node selectors, affinity, taints, tolerations and topology spread.
concepts.why: Staying up through failures and using special hardware both depend on putting pods in the right places.
concepts.body:
The scheduler first filters out nodes that can't run a pod (not enough unreserved resources, rules not met), then scores the rest and picks the best. You steer it with:

- `nodeSelector`: the simplest rule, node labels that must match (`kubernetes.io/os: linux`, `node.kubernetes.io/instance-type`, or your own `pool: gpu`).
- **Node affinity**: richer rules about node labels, either required (`requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution`, hard) or preferred, with weights (soft).
- **Pod affinity** and anti-affinity: place pods near or away from other pods with given labels, within a `topologyKey` such as the same node or the same **availability zone** (a separate data centre of a cloud region).

Taints keep pods away from nodes:

- A **taint** on a node (`dedicated=gpu:NoSchedule`) repels pods without a matching **toleration**. A toleration only allows a pod onto the node; add affinity if you also want to draw it there. `NoExecute` taints also evict pods that are already running.
- **Topology spread constraints** keep replicas evenly spread across zones and nodes, with `maxSkew` as the largest allowed difference. They're the usual tool for **high availability**: staying up when a node, or a whole zone, fails.

"IgnoredDuringExecution" means rules are checked only when a pod is placed; a running pod isn't moved if labels change later. The descheduler add-on can rebalance.

A **PriorityClass** gives pods a priority. When the cluster is full, a high-priority pending pod can trigger **preemption**: lower-priority pods are evicted to make room.

If a pod stays Pending, `kubectl describe` explains, with messages like `0/5 nodes are available: 3 node(s) had untolerated taint...`.
concepts.code:
spec:
  replicas: 6
  template:
    metadata: {labels: {app: api}}
    spec:
      topologySpreadConstraints:
        - maxSkew: 1
          topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone
          whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule
          labelSelector: {matchLabels: {app: api}}
      affinity:
        nodeAffinity:
          requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:
            nodeSelectorTerms:
              - matchExpressions:
                  - {key: pool, operator: In, values: [general]}
      tolerations:
        - {key: spot, operator: Equal, value: "true", effect: NoSchedule}
# kubectl taint nodes node-7 spot=true:NoSchedule
takeaways: nodeSelector and affinity attract; taints repel unless tolerated
Topology spread keeps replicas across zones
Rules apply only when a pod is placed
pitfalls: Adding a toleration and expecting pods to go to the tainted nodes: tolerations permit, they don't attract.

quiz.q: GPU nodes are tainted gpu=true:NoSchedule. How do you make a machine-learning pod run only on them?
options: A toleration plus a nodeSelector/affinity for the GPU label
quiz.explain: The toleration lets it onto GPU nodes; the selector keeps it off the others.

concepts.name: NetworkPolicies
concepts.summary: Restrict which pods may talk to which, starting from deny-all, enforced by the network plugin.
concepts.why: By default every pod can reach every other pod, so one hijacked pod can reach your database.
concepts.body:
Without policies the pod network is flat: any pod can connect to any other, in any namespace. A NetworkPolicy selects pods with `podSelector` and lists which traffic is allowed for them, in two directions: ingress (incoming connections) and egress (outgoing ones).

Rules to get right:

- Once any policy selects a pod for `Ingress` (or `Egress`), that direction becomes **default-deny** for it: only listed traffic is allowed. Policies are lists of what's allowed, and they add up.
- Allowed peers: `podSelector` (pods in the same namespace), `namespaceSelector` (whole namespaces, e.g. `kubernetes.io/metadata.name: monitoring`), both in one entry (pods with label X in namespaces Y), or `ipBlock` (a range of IP addresses).
- `ports` narrows by protocol (TCP or UDP) and port.
- Replies to allowed connections are allowed automatically.

A common starting point per namespace: one default-deny policy (`podSelector: {}` with `policyTypes: [Ingress, Egress]`), then explicit allows. If you deny egress, remember to allow DNS lookups (port 53, UDP and TCP, to kube-dns), or no name will resolve.

The policies are enforced by the network plugin (CNI). Calico, Cilium and most managed offerings enforce them; some simple plugins (like kind's default) don't, and then policies are silently ignored.

Standard NetworkPolicy looks only at addresses and ports (network "layers 3 and 4"). For rules about individual web requests, or for identities proven by certificates on both sides (mutual TLS), look at Cilium's own policies or a **service mesh**: small proxies placed beside every pod that handle traffic between services.
takeaways: Pods selected by any policy become default-deny for that direction
Policies only add allowed traffic
The network plugin must support NetworkPolicy; with egress denied, allow DNS
pitfalls: Applying an egress default-deny and breaking all DNS lookups.

quiz.q: Two policies select the db pods: one allows from app=api, one allows from app=worker. Which pods can connect?
quiz.explain: Policies add up: each one adds allowed sources.

concepts.name: Pod security contexts and admission
concepts.summary: Run containers as non-root with minimal rights, and enforce baseline or restricted security levels per namespace.
concepts.why: A container escape usually starts from a privileged or root container, and the defaults are too permissive.
concepts.body:
The **securityContext** (for the whole pod and per container) controls what a container may do:

- `runAsNonRoot: true`, `runAsUser: 10001`: never run as root, the all-powerful administrator (user ID 0).
- `allowPrivilegeEscalation: false`: a process can't gain more rights than it started with (for example through special programs marked to run as root).
- `readOnlyRootFilesystem: true`: the container can write only to mounted volumes (use an `emptyDir` for `/tmp`).
- `capabilities: {drop: ["ALL"]}`: Linux splits root's powers into separate **Linux capabilities** (change file owners, use ports below 1024...). Drop them all and add back only what's needed (`NET_BIND_SERVICE`).
- `seccompProfile: {type: RuntimeDefault}`: **seccomp** filters which **system calls** (requests to the kernel) the program may make, blocking rarely needed, risky ones.
- Never `privileged: true`, `hostPID`, `hostNetwork` or `hostPath` volumes for ordinary apps: they open the node itself to the container.

**Admission** is the step where the API server checks a new or changed object, after checking who you are and what you may do, and before saving it. **Pod Security Admission**, built in, checks new pods there against the Pod Security Standards, chosen per namespace with labels:

- `privileged`: no restrictions (for system namespaces),
- `baseline`: blocks the known ways to gain extra rights (privileged mode, host access, hostPath),
- `restricted`: requires the hardened settings above.

Each level can run in `enforce` (reject), `audit` (note it in the cluster's audit log) or `warn` (show a kubectl warning) mode, so you can introduce `restricted` gradually.

For your own rules (only images from approved registries, required labels, no `latest` tags) use ValidatingAdmissionPolicy, built in, with rules written in **CEL**, a small expression language; or a policy engine such as Kyverno or OPA Gatekeeper.
concepts.code:
# kubectl label ns shop pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted \
#   pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn=restricted
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata: {name: api, namespace: shop}
spec:
  securityContext:
    runAsNonRoot: true
    runAsUser: 10001
    seccompProfile: {type: RuntimeDefault}
  containers:
    - name: api
      image: ghcr.io/acme/api:2.1.0
      securityContext:
        allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
        readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
        capabilities: {drop: ["ALL"]}
      volumeMounts: [{name: tmp, mountPath: /tmp}]
  volumes: [{name: tmp, emptyDir: {}}]
takeaways: Non-root, no privilege escalation, drop all capabilities, read-only root file system, RuntimeDefault seccomp
Pod Security Admission: privileged, baseline or restricted per namespace
warn and audit modes let you roll out safely
pitfalls: Images that need root to start: build them to run as a non-root user instead of relaxing the namespace.

quiz.q: A namespace enforces restricted. A pod without allowPrivilegeEscalation: false is applied. What happens?
options: It runs but is evicted later
quiz.explain: enforce mode rejects pods that violate the level; warn and audit only report.

concepts.name: PodDisruptionBudgets and node drains
concepts.summary: Keep enough replicas up during planned disruptions like node upgrades with PodDisruptionBudgets.
concepts.why: Cluster upgrades and autoscalers evict pods; without a PDB they can take down a whole service at once.
concepts.body:
**Voluntary disruptions** are pod removals someone chose: emptying a node before maintenance with `kubectl drain`, cluster upgrades, an autoscaler removing a node. Involuntary ones are crashes, a node's operating system failing, or broken hardware.

A **PodDisruptionBudget** (PDB) limits voluntary disruptions for the pods matching its selector, with either `minAvailable` (e.g. `2` or `"50%"`) or `maxUnavailable`. Drains and autoscalers remove pods through the Eviction API, which refuses an eviction that would break the budget; the drain then waits and retries until replacement pods are ready elsewhere.

Points to know:

- PDBs don't protect against involuntary failures, and they don't stop a direct `kubectl delete pod` or a Deployment rollout (which has its own maxUnavailable).
- A PDB that can never be satisfied (`minAvailable: 1` on a one-replica Deployment, or `maxUnavailable: 0`) blocks drains forever, a classic cause of stuck node upgrades. Run at least two replicas of anything with a PDB.
- `unhealthyPodEvictionPolicy: AlwaysAllow` lets pods that are already unhealthy be evicted, so a broken app can't block maintenance.

To **drain** a node: `kubectl drain node-3 --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data` first cordons it (marks it so no new pods are placed there), then evicts its pods, respecting PDBs. `kubectl uncordon node-3` puts it back in service.
concepts.code:
apiVersion: policy/v1
kind: PodDisruptionBudget
metadata: {name: api}
spec:
  minAvailable: 2
  selector: {matchLabels: {app: api}}
  unhealthyPodEvictionPolicy: AlwaysAllow
# kubectl get pdb api
# NAME  MIN AVAILABLE  MAX UNAVAILABLE  ALLOWED DISRUPTIONS
# api   2              N/A              1      (3 healthy replicas)
#
# kubectl drain node-3 --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data
# evicting pod shop/api-6f-x1
# error when evicting ... would violate the pod's disruption budget (retrying)
takeaways: PDBs limit voluntary evictions (drains, upgrades, scale-down)
They don't cover crashes or direct deletes
A PDB that can't be satisfied blocks node drains
pitfalls: A PDB with minAvailable: 1 on a single-replica Deployment, which makes every node drain hang.

quiz.q: Which action does a PodDisruptionBudget protect against?
options: kubectl drain during a cluster upgrade
quiz.explain: Drains use the Eviction API, which checks PDBs; the others bypass it.

concepts.name: Troubleshooting pods systematically
concepts.summary: Diagnose Pending, ImagePullBackOff, CrashLoopBackOff, OOMKilled and not-ready pods with a fixed routine.
concepts.why: Most incidents are one of a handful of failure states, each with a known first check.
concepts.body:
Start from the pod's status and follow the matching path.

- **Pending**: not placed on a node yet. `describe` shows why: not enough unreserved CPU or memory (requests too big, or the cluster is full), a **taint** on the nodes (a mark that keeps pods away) that the pod has no **toleration** for, placement rules (affinity) that no node meets, or a storage claim (**PVC**) that can't be satisfied.
- **ContainerCreating** for a long time: storage can't be attached, a ConfigMap or Secret the pod needs is missing, or the network plugin has a problem. Check events.
- **ErrImagePull / ImagePullBackOff**: Kubernetes can't download the image. A wrong name or tag, a private registry without login details (`imagePullSecrets`), or the registry limiting how many downloads you may make.

The two most common failures of a pod that did start:

- **CrashLoopBackOff**: the container keeps exiting. Read `logs --previous` and the last exit code: 1 is an app error, 137 is SIGKILL (often OOMKilled), 143 is SIGTERM, 127 is "command not found" (a wrong `command` or `args`).
- **Running but 0/1 READY**: the readiness probe fails; its events show the web status code it got, or that it ran out of time.

**Running and ready but unreachable**: check the Service's endpoints (`kubectl get endpointslices`), its selector against the pod labels, `targetPort`, any NetworkPolicies, then DNS from a debug pod.

Habits: read events first, change one thing at a time, and look at the owning objects (Deployment, ReplicaSet) too. Some errors, such as an exceeded ResourceQuota, appear only on the ReplicaSet, because the pod was never created.
concepts.code:
kubectl get pods -o wide
kubectl describe pod api-7d9-k2 | tail -20           # events
kubectl get pod api-7d9-k2 -o jsonpath='{.status.containerStatuses[0].lastState}'
# {"terminated":{"exitCode":137,"reason":"OOMKilled",...}}

kubectl logs api-7d9-k2 --previous | tail
kubectl describe rs -l app=api | grep -A3 Events      # e.g. exceeded quota
kubectl get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=api
kubectl run net --rm -it --image=nicolaka/netshoot -- curl -sv http://api.shop
takeaways: Status tells you which path to follow
Exit codes: 137 SIGKILL/OOM, 143 SIGTERM, 127 command not found
Check endpoints, selectors and policies when ready pods are unreachable
pitfalls: Restarting things before reading the events and the previous logs, which destroys the evidence.

quiz.q: A pod is Running but shows READY 0/1, and the Service gets no traffic to it. What should you check first?
options: The readiness probe's failures in the pod's events
quiz.explain: 0/1 ready with Running means the readiness probe fails, which also removes it from endpoints.

concepts.name: Controllers, watches and reconciliation
concepts.summary: How controllers list and watch objects, queue work and reconcile, and why that design survives failures.
concepts.why: Understanding reconciliation explains how Kubernetes behaves under failure, and it's the basis for writing operators.
concepts.body:
Every controller follows the same loop: observe the desired and the actual state, compare them, act to close the gap, repeat. This is called **reconciliation**. It is **level-triggered**: it reacts to how things are now, not to the individual change notifications that led there. So a missed notification or a controller restart loses nothing; the next pass sees the same state and does the right thing.

How it works:

- A controller first lists all objects of its kind, then watches the API server: it keeps a connection open and receives every change after the version it listed (`resourceVersion`). In client-go, Kubernetes' official Go library, **informers** do this. They keep a local copy of the objects and call the controller's handlers on add, update and delete.
- The handlers only put object keys (`namespace/name`) on a **work queue**. Worker routines take keys off it and run `Reconcile(key)`, retrying failures with growing delays. A key that's already waiting isn't added twice, so bursts of changes don't pile up.

Safety rules:

- **Optimistic concurrency**: every write includes the object's `resourceVersion`. If someone else changed the object in the meantime, the API answers 409 Conflict, and the controller reads it again and retries. No locks are needed.
- **Owner references** link children to parents (ReplicaSet to Deployment, pod to ReplicaSet). Kubernetes' **garbage collector** deletes the children when the owner goes, either after it (background) or before it (foreground).
- **Finalizers** on an object block its deletion until a controller has cleaned up things outside the cluster (a cloud disk, a DNS record) and removed its finalizer. A finalizer nobody removes is why objects hang in Terminating.
- `metadata.generation` goes up on each spec change; controllers write `status.observedGeneration` so clients can tell whether the status already reflects the latest spec.

**Leader election** through Lease objects makes sure only one copy of a controller acts at a time; if it dies, another copy takes over.
concepts.code:
# Watch the raw stream of changes a controller sees
kubectl get deploy web --watch --output-watch-events -o name
# ADDED     deployment.apps/web
# MODIFIED  deployment.apps/web

kubectl get pod web-7c6d9f8b5-abcde -o jsonpath='{.metadata.ownerReferences[0].kind}'
# ReplicaSet
kubectl get deploy web -o jsonpath='{.metadata.generation} {.status.observedGeneration}'
# 7 7

# Why is this namespace stuck Terminating?
kubectl get ns old -o jsonpath='{.spec.finalizers} {.status.conditions[*].message}'
kubectl get lease -n kube-system     # leader election locks
takeaways: Level-triggered reconcile: act on the current state, survive missed notifications
Informers keep a local copy; work queues drop duplicates and retry
resourceVersion conflicts, owner references, finalizers, observedGeneration
pitfalls: Removing finalizers by hand to 'fix' a stuck delete, leaking the external resources they guarded.

quiz.q: Why is a controller that crashes and restarts unlikely to leave things inconsistent?
options: The API server replays every missed event exactly once
It reconciles from the current observed state, not from an event log
Pods pause while it is down
quiz.explain: Level-triggered design means the next reconcile computes what to do from present state.

concepts.name: CRDs and operators
concepts.summary: Extend the API with CustomResourceDefinitions, and automate running software with operator controllers.
concepts.why: Most platform tooling (cert-manager, Argo CD, database operators) is custom object types plus controllers.
concepts.body:
A **CustomResourceDefinition** (CRD) adds a new kind of object to the API server: a group, a kind, versions, and a **schema**, a description of the allowed fields, written in the OpenAPI v3 format, which the server uses to check objects. Once it's applied, `kubectl get certificates` works just like for a built-in kind, and RBAC, watching and storage in etcd come for free. Objects of such a kind are called **custom resources**.

CRD features worth knowing:

- Structural schemas with defaults, lists of allowed values, and `x-kubernetes-validations` rules written in **CEL**, a small rule language (e.g. `self.minReplicas <= self.maxReplicas`), checked by the API server.
- The `status` subresource separates writes to spec (by users) from writes to status (by the controller). The `scale` subresource makes autoscalers and `kubectl scale` work.
- `additionalPrinterColumns` choose what `kubectl get` shows.
- Several versions with one storage version. Converting between versions with different schemas needs a conversion **webhook**: a web service of yours that the API server calls to do it.

A CRD alone only stores data. An operator is a controller that reconciles those custom resources into real things: a `PostgresCluster` object becomes StatefulSets, Services, backups and failover logic. It captures what an experienced operations engineer would otherwise do by hand.

Operators are usually written in Go with the controller-runtime library, using the Kubebuilder or Operator SDK tooling, or in Python with kopf. The reconcile function should be **idempotent** (safe to run again), set owner references on what it creates, use finalizers for clean-up outside the cluster, and report progress as conditions in status.

Before writing one, check whether a ConfigMap plus a Job, or an existing operator, already solves the problem.
concepts.code:
apiVersion: apiextensions.k8s.io/v1
kind: CustomResourceDefinition
metadata: {name: backups.ops.example.com}
spec:
  group: ops.example.com
  names: {kind: Backup, plural: backups, singular: backup}
  scope: Namespaced
  versions:
    - name: v1
      served: true
      storage: true
      subresources: {status: {}}
      schema:
        openAPIV3Schema:
          type: object
          properties:
            spec:
              type: object
              required: [database, schedule]
              properties:
                database: {type: string}
                schedule: {type: string}
                keep: {type: integer, minimum: 1, default: 7}
# kubectl get backups   (a controller must still act on them)
takeaways: A CRD adds an API type with schema validation and CEL rules
An operator is a controller reconciling custom resources
Use status subresource, owner references, finalizers and conditions
pitfalls: Writing an operator for something a Helm chart or CronJob would handle.

quiz.q: You apply a CRD and create a custom resource, but nothing happens in the cluster. Why?
options: Custom resources must be in kube-system
A CRD only stores objects; a controller must act on them
quiz.explain: Behaviour comes from a controller watching the resource; the CRD only defines and stores it.

concepts.name: API requests, admission and server-side apply
concepts.summary: Follow a write through authentication, authorization, admission and etcd, and see who owns which field with server-side apply.
concepts.why: Webhooks, policy engines and apply conflicts all live on this path; it explains many confusing errors.
concepts.body:
Every write to the API server passes through fixed stages:

1. **Authentication**, who are you: client certificates, tokens (ServiceAccount tokens are signed JSON Web Tokens, **JWTs**; people's tokens often come from the company's login system through **OpenID Connect**, the standard behind "sign in with..." buttons) or an authentication webhook.
2. **Authorization**, may you do this: RBAC, plus the Node authorizer for kubelets and optional webhooks, checks the verb on the resource.
3. Mutating admission: built-in steps (filling in the default ServiceAccount, LimitRange defaults), mutating admission webhooks (for example, adding sidecar containers) and MutatingAdmissionPolicies may change the object.
4. Checking the object against its schema.
5. Validating admission: ResourceQuota, PodSecurity, ValidatingAdmissionPolicy (CEL rules, run inside the API server) and validating webhooks can reject it.
6. Saved to etcd, which gives it a new `resourceVersion`; watchers are notified.

An **admission webhook** is a web service of yours that the API server calls in step 3 or 5. That puts it on the critical path: a webhook that is down, with `failurePolicy: Fail`, can block all pod creation. Limit which objects it sees with selectors, set short timeouts, and exclude kube-system.

**Server-side apply** (`kubectl apply --server-side`) moves the merging of your manifest into the API server. It records field ownership in `metadata.managedFields`: each manager (kubectl, an HPA, Helm, a controller) owns the fields it set. Applying a different value for a field someone else owns is a conflict; you either drop the field from your file or use `--force-conflicts` to take it over. This is how a GitOps tool and an HPA can safely share one Deployment, as long as your manifest leaves out `replicas`.
concepts.code:
kubectl apply --server-side --field-manager=ci -f deploy.yaml
kubectl get deploy web --show-managed-fields -o yaml | grep -E 'manager:|operation:'
#   manager: ci                         operation: Apply
#   manager: kube-controller-manager    operation: Update
# Conflict example:
kubectl apply --server-side --field-manager=other -f deploy-replicas-5.yaml
# error: Apply failed with 1 conflict: conflict with "ci": .spec.replicas

kubectl get validatingwebhookconfigurations,mutatingwebhookconfigurations
kubectl get --raw /metrics | grep apiserver_admission_webhook_rejection_count | head -3
takeaways: Authentication, authorization, mutating admission, checks, validating admission, etcd
Webhooks can block the cluster: scope them and set timeouts
Server-side apply tracks field owners and reports conflicts
pitfalls: A cluster-wide failing webhook with failurePolicy: Fail that blocks even kube-system pods.

quiz.q: With server-side apply, your deploy pipeline's manifest sets replicas: 3 while an HPA manages replicas. What is the right fix?
options: Remove replicas from the pipeline's manifest
quiz.explain: Not declaring a field you don't want to own lets the HPA own it without conflicts.

concepts.name: kubelet, CRI and the pod sandbox
concepts.summary: How the kubelet turns a pod spec into containers via CRI, containerd, runc, cgroups and the pause sandbox.
concepts.why: Node-level failures, evictions and resource behaviour make sense only with this picture.
concepts.body:
The kubelet watches the pods assigned to its node and gives orders to the container runtime through the **Container Runtime Interface** (CRI), an API based on gRPC. Kubernetes 1.24 removed its built-in Docker adapter (dockershim), so nodes run containerd or CRI-O directly. Images built with Docker still work everywhere, because they follow the shared OCI image standard.

For each pod the kubelet first asks the runtime for a **pod sandbox**: a set of Linux namespaces (network; IPC, for shared memory; UTS, for the host name) kept alive by a tiny pause container. It calls the CNI plugin to give that sandbox its IP address. Each app container is then created by runc (or another low-level runtime such as gVisor or Kata, chosen through a RuntimeClass) inside the sandbox, sharing its network namespace. That's why containers in a pod share `localhost`, and why the IP address survives container restarts.

Resources map onto **cgroups** v2, the Linux feature that limits and measures groups of processes: a tree of `kubepods` groups per QoS class, then per pod and per container. Memory limits become `memory.max`; CPU requests become `cpu.weight`, and CPU limits `cpu.max`.

The kubelet also:

- runs probes, and restarts containers with growing delays (the CrashLoopBackOff wait),
- performs node-pressure eviction when memory, disk space or process IDs run low, choosing victims by QoS class and by how far they use more than they requested,
- cleans up unused images and dead containers,
- reports node status, and renews a Lease object every 10 seconds as its heartbeat ("I'm alive").

`crictl` talks CRI directly on a node, for debugging when the API can't help.
concepts.code:
# on a node (e.g. docker exec -it kind-worker bash)
crictl pods | head -3
# POD ID   CREATED  STATE  NAME            NAMESPACE
# 4b1c...  2h       Ready  web-7c6d9-abc   default
crictl ps --pod 4b1c                     # app containers of that sandbox
crictl inspectp 4b1c | grep -m1 '"ip"'   # sandbox IP from CNI

# cgroup of a Burstable pod (cgroup v2, systemd driver)
ls /sys/fs/cgroup/kubepods.slice/kubepods-burstable.slice/ | head -3
cat /sys/fs/cgroup/kubepods.slice/kubepods-burstable.slice/*/memory.max | head -1

journalctl -u kubelet --since -10m | grep -i evict
takeaways: kubelet speaks CRI to containerd/CRI-O; runc creates containers
The pause sandbox holds the pod's shared namespaces and IP
Requests and limits become cgroup v2 weights and maxima; kubelet evicts under pressure
pitfalls: Thinking Kubernetes still needs Docker on nodes; it uses containerd or CRI-O directly.

quiz.q: Why does a pod keep its IP when its app container restarts?
options: The IP belongs to the pod sandbox's network namespace, not the app container
The kubelet reserves it in etcd
quiz.explain: The pod sandbox (held by the pause container) owns the network namespace, so restarting app containers doesn't change it.

concepts.name: Service networking internals
concepts.summary: How kube-proxy (iptables, IPVS, nftables) or eBPF tools make Service addresses work on top of the pod network.
concepts.why: Debugging odd delays, dropped connections or lost client addresses requires knowing what the packets really do.
concepts.body:
The **Kubernetes network model** requires every pod to have its own IP address and to reach every other pod directly, without its address being rewritten on the way. The CNI plugin makes this true in one of three styles: an **overlay network** (pod traffic wrapped inside ordinary traffic between nodes, using VXLAN or Geneve), routed networks (nodes announce their pod address ranges to the network's routers using BGP, as Calico can), or pod addresses taken straight from the cloud's own private network (AWS VPC CNI, Azure CNI).

A ClusterIP isn't attached to any network card. kube-proxy on each node watches Services and EndpointSlices and programs the Linux kernel so that packets sent to `ClusterIP:port` have their destination rewritten to one ready pod. That rewriting is a form of **NAT**, network address translation (here DNAT, for destination):

- **iptables** mode: iptables is Linux's classic system of packet rules. One chain of rules per Service picks a pod at random; updating the rules gets slow with many thousands of Services.
- IPVS mode: the kernel's built-in load balancer, using hash tables and offering more balancing methods.
- nftables mode (stable since 1.33): the modern successor to iptables mode, with faster updates.

**eBPF**-based tools such as Cilium can replace kube-proxy entirely. eBPF runs small, checked programs inside the kernel, so the translation happens even earlier: when a connection is opened, or as a packet arrives.

Consequences:

- Balancing is per **connection**, not per request. Long-lived connections, as used by HTTP/2 and gRPC, stick to one pod. Balance in the client instead (with a headless Service), or use a service mesh.
- Traffic from outside through a NodePort or LoadBalancer Service may hop to another node and have its source address rewritten (SNAT), hiding the client's IP. `externalTrafficPolicy: Local` keeps the client IP and avoids the hop, but then only nodes running a matching pod receive traffic.
- `internalTrafficPolicy` and topology-aware routing can keep traffic inside one zone, saving cross-zone costs.

# On a node using kube-proxy in iptables mode:
iptables -t nat -L KUBE-SERVICES -n | grep shop/api
# KUBE-SVC-XYZ  tcp -- 0.0.0.0/0  10.96.112.7  /* shop/api:http cluster IP */ tcp dpt:80
iptables -t nat -L KUBE-SVC-XYZ -n
# KUBE-SEP-AAA  statistic mode random probability 0.33333
# KUBE-SEP-BBB  statistic mode random probability 0.50000
# KUBE-SEP-CCC
kubectl -n kube-system get cm kube-proxy -o yaml | grep -m1 'mode:'

# preserve client source IPs for an external Service
kubectl patch svc web -p '{"spec":{"externalTrafficPolicy":"Local"}}'
takeaways: The CNI plugin gives pods routable addresses; kube-proxy or eBPF makes ClusterIPs work
Balancing is per connection: watch out with gRPC and HTTP/2
externalTrafficPolicy: Local keeps the client IP and avoids an extra hop
pitfalls: Expecting a ClusterIP to spread gRPC requests across pods when clients hold one long connection.
